• Manifestations: Severe symmetrical proximal hypotonia ('floppy infant'), tongue fasciculations, bell-shaped chest from intercostal muscle weakness (sparing diaphragm), and death from respiratory failure before age 2 without treatment.
• Treatment: Nusinersen (antisense oligonucleotide promoting inclusion of exon 7 in SMN2 pre-mRNA) or Onasemnogene abeparvovec (gene replacement therapy).

stem: During a neurological exam, deep tendon reflexes are tested to evaluate the integrity of the spinal reflex arc. Testing the Achilles tendon reflex (ankle jerk) primarily evaluates which spinal nerve root?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. S1-S2.

Spinal reflex arc nerve roots (remember the counting mnemonic: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8):
• S1, S2: Achilles reflex (ankle jerk)
• L3, L4: Patellar reflex (knee jerk)
• C5, C6: Biceps and Brachioradialis reflexes
• C7, C8: Triceps reflex

stem: An adult male sustains an acute spinal cord transection at the T4 level following a motor vehicle crash. Immediately following the injury, he exhibits spinal shock. Which of the following sets of physiological findings characterizes the phase of acute spinal shock?

options.text: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, and sustained ankle clonus
Flaccid paralysis, absent deep tendon reflexes, loss of autonomic tone, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence
Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes with preserved sensation
Severe hypertension and tachycardia from sympathetic storm

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Flaccid paralysis, absent deep tendon reflexes, loss of autonomic tone, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence.

Immediately following acute traumatic spinal cord transection, the patient enters spinal shock, characterized by temporary loss of all cord functions below the lesion:
• Complete flaccid paralysis and areflexia (due to sudden loss of descending facilitatory supraspinal drive).
• Loss of autonomic tone (neurogenic shock: hypotension, bradycardia from loss of sympathetic output T1-L2).
• Atonic, flaccid bladder with overflow incontinence and absent anal sphincter tone.
After several days to weeks, spinal shock resolves and transitions into chronic upper motor neuron findings: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, and a hyperreflexic/spastic neurogenic bladder.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with subacute onset of bilateral lower extremity weakness, numbness from her umbilicus down to her toes, and urinary urgency. Sensation to pinprick, temperature, and light touch is completely absent below the T10 dermatome. Spinal MRI shows a focal, high-signal T2 lesion with gadolinium enhancement spanning more than two vertebral segments across the thoracic cord. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated IgG index. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Acute transverse myelitis.

Acute Transverse Myelitis is an inflammatory, immune-mediated demyelinating disorder affecting the entire cross-section of the spinal cord (most commonly thoracic):
• Clinical presentation: Rapidly progressive bilateral motor weakness, a sharply defined sensory level (umbilicus = T10 dermatome), and sphincter dysfunction (urinary urgency/retention).
• Etiology: Idiopathic post-infectious, or associated with multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica (anti-AQP4), or systemic lupus erythematosus.
• MRI: T2 hyperintensity with patchy gadolinium enhancement extending across the spinal cord cross-section.

stem: The spinal cord ends caudally as the conus medullaris. At which vertebral level does the conus medullaris terminate in the normal adult?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. L1–L2.

In adults, the conus medullaris (the tapered lower end of the spinal cord) typically terminates at the level of the L1-L2 intervertebral disc space (range: T12 to lower L2). The dural sac and subarachnoid space continue down to the level of S2. This anatomical arrangement creates the lumbar cistern (between L2 and S2), which contains only the cauda equina and CSF, allowing safe insertion of a lumbar puncture needle at L3-L4 or L4-L5 without injuring the spinal cord.

stem: Which fibrous strand of connective tissue is derived from the pia mater, extends from the tip of the conus medullaris through the lumbar cistern, and fuses with the dura mater at S2 to anchor the spinal cord to the coccyx?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Filum terminale.

The filum terminale is a delicate filament of fibrous tissue extending from the apex of the conus medullaris to the coccyx:
• Filum terminale internum: Upper portion within the dural sac, composed of pia mater bathed in CSF.
• Filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament): Lower portion outside the dural sac (below S2), composed of fused pia and dura mater, anchoring the spinal cord to the dorsum of the coccyx.
Tethered cord syndrome occurs when an abnormally thick or tight filum terminale restricts physiological motion of the spinal cord.

stem: In the spinal cord white matter, the lateral corticospinal tract contains descending motor axons organized somatotopically. Which of the following correctly describes the somatotopic arrangement of fibers in the lateral corticospinal tract from medial to lateral?

options.text: Sacral fibers are medial; Cervical fibers are lateral

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cervical → Thoracic → Lumbar → Sacral.

In both the lateral corticospinal tract and the spinothalamic tract, fibers are laminated somatotopically:
• Lateral corticospinal tract: Cervical fibers lie most MEDIALLY (nearest the gray matter), while Sacral fibers lie most LATERALLY (nearest the cord surface). This explains why a central cord injury (hyperextension) selectively damages medial/cervical fibers, paralyzing the arms while sparing the legs.
• Spinothalamic tract: Cervical fibers are MEDIAL, while sacral fibers are LATERAL. Extrinsic compression of the cord (e.g., meningioma) compresses the superficial sacral fibers first, causing sensory loss starting at the feet and ascending.

stem: A 5-year-old unvaccinated boy in a developing country develops a febrile illness followed by asymmetric flaccid paralysis of his right leg. Physical examination shows 0/5 strength in the right quadriceps and tibialis anterior with absent patellar and Achilles reflexes. Sensation is completely intact throughout both legs. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals a positive enterovirus PCR. Poliovirus causes pure motor deficits by selectively infecting and destroying which cells?

options.text: Alpha motor neurons in the anterior (ventral) horns of the spinal cord
Dorsal root ganglion sensory pseudounipolar neurons
Schwann cells in the peripheral motor nerves
Pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Alpha motor neurons in the anterior (ventral) horns of the spinal cord.

Poliovirus (a single-stranded, positive-sense, non-enveloped RNA picornavirus) selectively targets and replicates in the anterior (ventral) horn alpha motor neurons of the spinal cord (and motor nuclei of the brainstem). Destruction of these lower motor neurons results in asymmetric flaccid paralysis, severe muscle atrophy, and areflexia, with complete preservation of sensory pathways.

stem: Which specialized ligament consists of 21 pairs of tooth-like triangular lateral extensions of pia mater that pass through the arachnoid to anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater, separating the anterior and posterior nerve roots?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Denticulate ligament.

The denticulate ligaments (ligamenta denticulata) are bilateral, ribbon-like lateral shelves of pia mater with 21 tooth-like pointed processes extending from the foramen magnum down to T12-L1. They pierce the arachnoid to attach to the inner surface of the dura mater, suspending the spinal cord within the thecal sac and serving as a crucial surgical landmark separating dorsal sensory roots from ventral motor roots.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with chronic neck pain and numbness radiating down his right thumb. Examination shows weakness of right elbow flexion and forearm supination, along with a diminished right biceps and brachioradialis reflex. Sensation to pinprick is diminished over the right lateral forearm and thumb. Which cervical intervertebral disc herniation and nerve root is involved?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. C5-C6 disc compressing C6 root.

Cervical radiculopathy features:
• In the cervical spine, spinal nerves exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebrae (C1 exits above C1, C6 exits between C5 and C6, C8 exits between C7 and T1). Thus, a C5-C6 herniation compresses the exiting C6 nerve root.
• C6 radiculopathy findings: Sensory loss in the lateral forearm and thumb; motor weakness of biceps and brachioradialis (elbow flexion); diminished biceps and brachioradialis reflexes.
• In comparison, C7 radiculopathy causes numbness of the middle finger, triceps weakness, and diminished triceps reflex.

stem: In the spinal cord, preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies are located in the intermediolateral (IML) cell column of the lateral horn. Across which spinal cord segments is the intermediolateral cell column present?

options.text: Entire length of the spinal cord (C1 to Co1)

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. T1 to L2.

The autonomic nervous system anatomy:
• Sympathetic division (thoracolumbar outflow): Preganglionic cell bodies reside in the intermediolateral (IML) nucleus of the lateral horn from T1 to L2 (or L3).
• Parasympathetic division (craniosacral outflow): Preganglionic cell bodies reside in cranial nerve nuclei (CN III, VII, IX, X) and sacral cord segments S2, S3, S4.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with severe shooting pain down her right buttock, posterior thigh, calf, and sole of the foot. Examination shows weakness of right foot plantarflexion (inability to stand on tiptoes) and an absent right Achilles tendon reflex. Sensation to pinprick is diminished over the lateral border of the right foot and fifth digit. An MRI will most likely demonstrate a herniated disc compressing which nerve root?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. S1.

S1 radiculopathy (typically caused by an L5-S1 posterolateral disc herniation):
• Motor: Weakness of gastrocnemius/soleus (plantarflexion of the foot; patient cannot stand on toes).
• Reflex: Absent Achilles tendon (ankle jerk) reflex.
• Sensory: Numbness/pain along the posterior calf, sole of the foot, lateral foot, and little toe.
• In contrast, L5 radiculopathy affects foot dorsiflexion / heel walking (extensor hallucis longus) and sensation over the dorsum of the foot and big toe, with normal reflexes.

stem: A 22-year-old athlete sustains a severe spinal cord injury at T1. Several weeks later, full bladder distension triggers paroxysmal episodes of severe hypertension (blood pressure 210/115 mm Hg), pounding headache, profuse diaphoresis and flushing above the level of T1, and cold, pale skin with piloerection below T1. The heart rate is 45 bpm. What life-threatening syndrome is this patient experiencing?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Autonomic dysreflexia (hyperreflexia).

Autonomic Dysreflexia occurs in patients with spinal cord lesions at or above T6:
• Trigger: Noxious visceral stimuli below the lesion (most commonly bladder distension, catheter obstruction, or fecal impaction).
• Mechanism: Massive, uninhibited sympathetic discharge from the isolated splanchnic vascular bed causes severe vasoconstriction and acute hypertension.
• Response: Carotid baroreceptors detect severe hypertension and stimulate parasympathetic vagal output (producing reflex bradycardia) and cutaneous vasodilation above the lesion (flushing, sweating). However, inhibitory descending central signals cannot cross the T6 cord lesion, leaving uninhibited sympathetic vasoconstriction below the lesion.

stem: Which nucleus in the spinal cord gray matter extends from C8 to L3 (Rexed lamina VII), contains cell bodies of second-order neurons that receive unconscious proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs of the lower body, and gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Clarke column (nucleus dorsalis).

Clarke column (nucleus dorsalis / thoracicus) is located in the medial base of the dorsal horn (Rexed lamina VII) between spinal levels C8 and L3:
• Function: Relays unconscious proprioceptive signals from lower limb muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs.
• Axons project ipsilaterally to form the Dorsal Spinocerebellar Tract, ascending to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to coordinate lower extremity motor execution.

stem: A 25-year-old carpenter accidentally hits his thumb with a hammer. Immediately, he feels an intense, sharp, well-localized pain, followed several seconds later by a persistent, dull, throbbing, poorly localized ache. Which of the following pairs of primary sensory nerve fibers is responsible for transmitting the initial sharp pain versus the subsequent dull aching pain, respectively?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. A-delta fibers; C fibers.

Dual pain transmission:
• 'Fast pain' (first pain): Transmitted by lightly myelinated A-delta fibers (conduction velocity 5-30 m/s). It is sharp, pricking, rapid, and well-localized, terminating primarily in Rexed lamina I and V of the spinal cord dorsal horn.
• 'Slow pain' (second pain): Transmitted by unmyelinated C fibers (conduction velocity 0.5-2 m/s). It is dull, burning, aching, and poorly localized, terminating primarily in Rexed lamina II (substantia gelatinosa).

stem: Second-order nociceptive projection neurons of the spinothalamic tract originate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Where do the axons of these second-order neurons cross the midline to enter the contralateral anterolateral column?

options.text: Sensory decussation in the caudal medulla
Anterior white commissure, ascending 1–2 spinal segments as they cross
Posterior gray commissure at the exact segment of entry
Pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Anterior white commissure, ascending 1–2 spinal segments as they cross.

Primary nociceptive afferents enter the spinal cord, ascend or descend 1-2 segments in the tract of Lissauer (dorsolateral fasciculus), and synapse in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa / Rexed laminae I, II, V). The axons of second-order spinothalamic neurons then cross the midline obliquely through the anterior white commissure over 1 to 2 spinal segments before ascending in the contralateral anterolateral funiculus. This explains why an anterior cord lesion or syringomyelia selectively abolishes bilateral pain and temperature sensation.

stem: Immediately after bumping his elbow against a wall, a man vigorously rubs the injured area with his hand, which significantly reduces the perceived sharpness of the pain. According to the Gate Control Theory of pain proposed by Melzack and Wall, which of the following mechanisms accounts for this pain relief?

options.text: Activation of descending noradrenergic projections from the locus coeruleus
Activation of large myelinated A-beta fibers stimulating inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa
Direct depletion of substance P from peripheral nociceptors
Inhibition of NMDA receptors by magnesium in the thalamus
Upregulation of opioid receptors on peripheral free nerve endings

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Activation of large myelinated A-beta fibers stimulating inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa.

The Gate Control Theory of pain states that transmission of pain through dorsal horn projection neurons can be modulated locally:
• Noxious inputs via C-fibers activate projection neurons and inhibit local inhibitory interneurons, 'opening the gate.'
• Non-noxious mechanical tactile stimulation (rubbing, shaking) activates large-diameter myelinated A-beta fibers.
• A-beta collaterals excite local GABAergic/enkephalinergic inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II).
• These interneurons presynaptically and postsynaptically inhibit the transmission of pain signals to ascending spinothalamic projection neurons, 'closing the gate.'

stem: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain plays a central role in the endogenous descending pain-modulatory pathway. Electrical stimulation of the PAG produces profound analgesia. The PAG exerts this analgesic effect primarily by sending excitatory projections to which serotonergic brainstem nucleus in the rostral ventromedial medulla?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Nucleus raphe magnus.

Descending pain inhibition pathway:
1. Neurons in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain project to the rostral ventromedial medulla, specifically the nucleus raphe magnus (serotonergic) and the locus coeruleus (noradrenergic).
2. Nucleus raphe magnus axons descend in the dorsolateral funiculus of the spinal cord to the dorsal horn.
3. They release serotonin (and norepinephrine), which excites local enkephalinergic inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa.
4. Enkephalin binds to presynaptic mu-opioid receptors on primary afferent C-fibers (inhibiting Ca2+ influx and substance P release) and postsynaptic receptors on projection neurons (hyperpolarizing them via K+ efflux).

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with severe burning pain across his right flank 3 months after a vesicular rash in the same dermatome resolved (postherpetic neuralgia). Even the light touch of a cotton shirt against his skin causes agonizing, intolerable pain. Which of the following terms correctly defines the perception of pain from an ordinarily non-painful stimulus?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Allodynia.

Definitions of pain terms:
• Allodynia: Pain resulting from a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain (e.g., light touch of clothing triggering intense pain in postherpetic neuralgia or trigeminal neuralgia).
• Hyperalgesia: Increased pain sensitivity to a stimulus that is normally painful (e.g., mild pinprick feeling intensely agonizing).
• Paresthesia: An abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked, not unpleasant (e.g., tingling, 'pins and needles').
• Dysesthesia: An unpleasant abnormal sensation (spontaneous or evoked).

stem: Capsaicin, the chemical compound responsible for the heat of chili peppers, is applied topically to manage neuropathic pain. Capsaicin selectively binds to and activates which specialized heat- and acid-sensitive non-selective cation channel on nociceptive nerve endings?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. TRPV1 (Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1).

TRPV1 is a non-selective cation channel expressed on nociceptive A-delta and C fibers that is gated by noxious heat (>43°C), extracellular protons (acidosis / pH < 5.9), and capsaicin. 
• Therapeutic mechanism of topical capsaicin: Initial application causes burning pain by opening TRPV1; chronic repeated application causes massive sustained Ca2+ influx that overloads mitochondria and depletes substance P, leading to prolonged defunctionalization and desensitization of nociceptive terminals.

stem: A 58-year-old man experiencing an acute myocardial infarction presents with crushing retrosternal chest pressure that radiates to his left neck, jaw, and the medial aspect of his left arm. What neuroanatomical mechanism explains why visceral pain from the heart is referred to these specific somatic dermatomes?

options.text: Direct electrical ephaptic transmission between autonomic and somatic peripheral nerves
Convergence of cardiac visceral afferents and somatic cutaneous afferents on the same second-order dorsal horn neurons at T1–T4
Retrograde axonal transport of substance P from cardiac nerves to the brachial plexus
Infarction of the medial lemniscus within the caudal brainstem
Spillover of noradrenaline in the sympathetic chain ganglia

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Convergence of cardiac visceral afferents and somatic cutaneous afferents on the same second-order dorsal horn neurons at T1–T4.

Referred pain occurs due to convergence-projection in the spinal cord dorsal horn:
• Visceral nociceptive afferents from the ischemic myocardium travel with sympathetic nerves to enter upper thoracic spinal cord segments (T1-T4/T5).
• Somatic cutaneous sensory afferents from the chest wall and medial arm (T1-T4 dermatomes) enter the exact same spinal segments.
• Both visceral and somatic fibers converge onto the same second-order spinothalamic projection neurons.
• Because the cerebral cortex has vastly more prior experience processing somatic cutaneous inputs, it misinterprets the ascending visceral nociceptive activity as arising from the somatic dermatomes.

stem: Which of the following pro-inflammatory neuropeptides is stored alongside glutamate in dense-core vesicles of primary nociceptive C-fibers, is released into the dorsal horn upon high-frequency noxious stimulation, and binds to neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptors to mediate slow, long-lasting pain transmission and central sensitization?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Substance P.

Substance P is an 11-amino acid neuropeptide synthesized in dorsal root ganglion cells and transported to primary nociceptive C-fiber terminals. 
• In the spinal cord dorsal horn, substance P is coreleased with glutamate in response to intense, repetitive noxious stimuli, binding to postsynaptic Neurokinin-1 (NK-1) receptors to produce prolonged depolarization and initiate central sensitization ('wind-up').
• Peripherally, substance P causes neurogenic inflammation: arteriolar vasodilation and mast cell degranulation (histamine release), producing edema and hyperalgesia.

stem: Following tissue injury, uninjured skin surrounding the primary wound site becomes hypersensitive to touch and mild thermal stimuli. This secondary hyperalgesia and 'wind-up' phenomenon in the spinal cord dorsal horn is mediated by continuous activation of which postsynaptic receptor leading to calcium influx?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. NMDA receptor.

Central sensitization ('wind-up') is an activity-dependent increase in neuronal excitability in the dorsal horn:
• Repetitive C-fiber firing causes sustained release of glutamate and substance P, leading to prolonged baseline depolarization via AMPA and NK-1 receptors.
• This sustained depolarization repels the resting Mg2+ block from NMDA receptors.
• Unblocked NMDA receptors allow massive Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic neurons, activating protein kinase C (PKC) and nitric oxide synthase (NOS).
• This increases synaptic strength (long-term potentiation of pain pathways), expanding receptive fields and causing secondary hyperalgesia.

stem: Which cortical and limbic structures receive ascending nociceptive projections from the intralaminar and medial thalamic nuclei (paleospinothalamic tract), mediating the unpleasant, emotional, and affective suffering of pain rather than its sensory-discriminative localization?

options.text: Primary motor cortex and supplementary motor area
Anterior cingulate cortex and insular cortex
Primary visual cortex and lingual gyrus
Inferior temporal gyrus and fusiform gyrus

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Anterior cingulate cortex and insular cortex.

The pain pathway bifurcates in the brain:
1. Lateral pain system (spinothalamic → VPL thalamus → primary somatosensory cortex S1/S2): Mediates sensory-discriminative aspects (location, intensity, duration, and quality of pain).
2. Medial pain system (spinoreticular / paleospinothalamic → medial thalamus → anterior cingulate cortex [ACC] and anterior insula): Mediates motivational-affective suffering, autonomic arousal, and emotional unpleasantness of pain. Patients with lesions of the ACC perceive that pain is present but are no longer distressed or bothered by it ('pain asymbolia').

stem: A 50-year-old man with intractable cancer pain undergoes a percutaneous cordotomy to achieve pain relief. The neurosurgeon surgically transects which ascending tract in the spinal cord anterolateral column contralateral to the painful region?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Lateral spinothalamic tract.

A cordotomy is a neurosurgical procedure used for unilateral intractable cancer pain below the neck. The lateral spinothalamic tract in the anterolateral quadrant of the spinal cord is ablated CONTRALATERAL to the site of pain (since spinothalamic axons decussate in the anterior white commissure 1-2 segments above their entry level).

stem: Rexed laminae divide the spinal cord gray matter into ten distinct histological zones from dorsal to ventral. Which Rexed lamina corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa, which receives dense terminations from primary unmyelinated C-fibers and serves as a major site of pain gating?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Lamina II (substantia gelatinosa).

• Lamina I: Marginal zone (receives A-delta and C fibers; origin of some spinothalamic projection neurons).
• Lamina II: Substantia gelatinosa of Rolando (high density of interneurons regulating pain transmission; primary site of opiate receptors and gate-control inhibition).
• Laminae III and IV: Nucleus proprius (mechanoreceptive input).
• Lamina V: Deep dorsal horn containing wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons that receive convergent tactile and nociceptive inputs.
• Lamina IX: Ventral horn alpha and gamma motor neurons.

stem: Which cold-activated TRP ion channel is expressed on sensory nerve endings, is activated by moderate cool temperatures (10–28°C) as well as by menthol and icilin, and imparts the familiar cooling sensation of peppermint?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. TRPM8.

TRPM8 (Transient Receptor Potential Melastatin 8) is a non-selective cation channel on sensory afferents activated by cool temperatures (10-28°C) and cooling chemical agonists like menthol, eucalyptol, and icilin. Activation produces the perception of coldness and can produce analgesia via gate-control mechanisms.

stem: During tissue injury and inflammation, a chemical 'inflammatory soup' is released that sensitizes peripheral nociceptors (peripheral sensitization). Which of the following inflammatory mediators binds to Gs-coupled receptors to increase intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) and activate protein kinase A (PKA), lowering the activation threshold of voltage-gated Nav1.8 sodium channels?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2).

Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), synthesized by cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) at sites of inflammation, binds to EP2 and EP4 Gs-coupled receptors on nociceptive nerve terminals. This activates adenylyl cyclase, elevating intracellular cAMP and activating Protein Kinase A (PKA). PKA phosphorylates tetrodotoxin-resistant voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.8 and Nav1.9) and TRPV1, lowering their activation thresholds and causing peripheral sensitization (primary hyperalgesia). NSAIDs relieve inflammatory pain by inhibiting COX-2, preventing PGE2 synthesis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with severe fibromyalgia complains of widespread musculoskeletal aching and fatigue. Functional neuroimaging demonstrates normal peripheral nerve function but exaggerated activity in the insula and anterior cingulate cortex during low-intensity pressure stimuli. This central amplification of pain perception without ongoing peripheral tissue damage is classified as:
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Nociplastic pain.

Mechanistic classifications of pain (IASP):
1. Nociceptive pain: Arises from actual or threatened damage to non-neural tissue and activation of nociceptors (e.g., osteoarthritis, burn, bone fracture).
2. Neuropathic pain: Caused by a demonstrable lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system (e.g., diabetic polyneuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, spinal cord injury).
3. Nociplastic pain: Pain arising from altered nociception despite no clear evidence of actual or threatened tissue damage or somatosensory lesion (e.g., fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, tension headache, chronic widespread pain). It is characterized by central sensitization and augmented CNS sensory processing.

stem: A 60-year-old man with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy is started on duloxetine. Duloxetine relieves neuropathic pain primarily by which mechanism of action in the central nervous system?

options.text: Direct agonism at mu-opioid receptors in the dorsal horn
Inhibiting reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, enhancing descending pain-inhibitory pathways
Direct blockade of NMDA glutamate receptors
Antagonism of voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral axons

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Inhibiting reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, enhancing descending pain-inhibitory pathways.

Duloxetine is a Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor (SNRI) approved for diabetic neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia. It blocks the presynaptic transporters for both norepinephrine (NET) and serotonin (SERT). By increasing synaptic concentrations of norepinephrine and serotonin in the spinal cord dorsal horn, it potentiates the endogenous descending inhibitory pain pathways (from locus coeruleus and nucleus raphe magnus), suppressing spinal nociceptive transmission.

stem: Pregabalin and gabapentin are first-line medications for neuropathic pain. Despite their chemical similarity to GABA, they do not bind to GABA receptors. What is their true pharmacological target?

options.text: Alpha-2-delta (α2δ) auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Alpha-2-delta (α2δ) auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels.

Gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) bind with high affinity to the alpha-2-delta-1 (α2δ-1) auxiliary subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels in the dorsal horn and brain. This binding disrupts channel trafficking to the presynaptic terminal, decreasing calcium influx upon action potential arrival and thereby reducing the exocytotic release of excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate, substance P, and CGRP) from sensitized primary afferents.

stem: Bradykinin is one of the most potent endogenous algogenic (pain-producing) substances generated during tissue damage. Bradykinin is cleaved from high-molecular-weight kininogen by which plasma enzyme?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Kallikrein.

During tissue injury and coagulation cascade activation, factor XIIa converts prekallikrein to active kallikrein. Kallikrein then cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen (HMWK) to release bradykinin (a 9-amino acid peptide). Bradykinin binds to Gq-coupled B2 receptors on nociceptive terminals, activating PLC and PKC to directly depolarize nociceptors and sensitize TRPV1 channels, producing intense burning pain, vasodilation, and vascular permeability.

stem: Which bundle of small-diameter unmyelinated and thinly myelinated axons is located at the apex of the spinal cord dorsal horn, allowing primary pain and temperature afferents to ascend or descend 1–2 vertebral segments before synapsing in the gray matter?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Tract of Lissauer (dorsolateral fasciculus).

The tract of Lissauer (posterolateral tract) lies capping the dorsal horn between the substantia gelatinosa and the surface of the spinal cord. It contains bifurcating primary afferent fibers (A-delta and C fibers) that travel rostrally or caudally 1 to 2 segments before penetrating the dorsal horn gray matter (Rexed laminae I, II, and V). This intersegmental spread contributes to the overlap of sensory dermatomes.

stem: Wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons located in lamina V of the dorsal horn respond to both non-noxious low-threshold tactile stimuli and high-threshold noxious stimuli. What unique firing characteristic enables WDR neurons to signal stimulus intensity across the entire spectrum from light brush to intense pain?

options.text: All-or-none burst firing only at supramaximal stimuli
Monotonic increase in action potential discharge frequency proportional to stimulus intensity
Rapid complete adaptation within 50 milliseconds of stimulus onset
Spontaneous rhythmic oscillation independent of input
Selective response only to cold temperatures below 0°C

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Monotonic increase in action potential discharge frequency proportional to stimulus intensity.

Wide Dynamic Range (WDR) neurons in lamina V receive convergent polysynaptic inputs from A-beta (light touch), A-delta, and C fibers (noxious). Unlike nociceptive-specific (NS) neurons in lamina I which fire only when tissue damage occurs, WDR neurons increase their action potential firing frequency graded proportionally to increasing mechanical pressure, encoding both tactile intensity and the transition into noxious pain. They are also central to the wind-up phenomenon and convergence in referred pain.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with paroxysms of severe, sharp, electric shock-like pain shooting across her right cheek and lower jaw (V2 and V3 distribution). The pain lasts 10 to 15 seconds at a time and is triggered by light touch, brushing her teeth, or a cold gust of wind. Neurological examination is completely normal with no sensory loss. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for this disorder?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Carbamazepine.

This patient has Trigeminal Neuralgia (tic douloureux):
• Classic presentation: Brief, paroxysmal, lancinating, electric-shock pain in the distribution of CN V2/V3, triggered by innocuous tactile stimuli (touch, chewing, shaving, wind).
• Pathophysiology: Neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant arterial loop (most commonly the superior cerebellar artery), causing focal demyelination and ephaptic cross-talk between tactile and nociceptive axons.
• First-line medical therapy: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine), which blocks use-dependent voltage-gated sodium channels, suppressing high-frequency neuronal firing. (Monitor for aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, SIADH, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome).

stem: During a neurological examination, the physician tests the corneal reflex by touching a wisp of sterile cotton to the right cornea. Both the right and left eyes blink symmetrically. Which cranial nerves serve as the afferent and efferent limbs of this reflex, respectively?

options.text: Afferent: CN V1 (Ophthalmic); Efferent: CN VII (Facial)
Afferent: CN II (Optic); Efferent: CN III (Oculomotor)
Afferent: CN V2 (Maxillary); Efferent: CN VII (Facial)
Afferent: CN VII (Facial); Efferent: CN V1 (Ophthalmic)
Afferent: CN V1 (Ophthalmic); Efferent: CN III (Oculomotor)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Afferent: CN V1 (Ophthalmic); Efferent: CN VII (Facial).

The corneal reflex pathway:
• Afferent limb: Nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1) senses mechanical stimulation on the cornea.
• Central relay: Enters the pons, descends to the spinal trigeminal nucleus, and sends bilateral interneuronal projections via the reticular formation to the facial motor nuclei (CN VII) in both the ipsilateral and contralateral pons.
• Efferent limb: CN VII motor fibers innervate the orbicularis oculi muscles bilaterally, producing both a direct blink (stimulated eye) and a consensual blink (opposite eye).

stem: Which of the following sensory nuclei of the trigeminal nerve contains primary pseudounipolar sensory cell bodies located entirely inside the central nervous system (rather than in a peripheral ganglion) and mediates proprioception from the muscles of mastication, periodontal ligaments, and teeth?

options.text: Mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve
Chief (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve
Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.

The mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (located in the lateral periaqueductal gray of the midbrain and rostral pons) is unique in neuroanatomy: it is the ONLY structure in the CNS that contains primary sensory pseudounipolar cell bodies (derived embryologically from neural crest cells that failed to migrate outside the neural tube). It receives proprioceptive inputs from muscle spindles in the muscles of mastication (jaw jerk reflex) and mechanoreceptors in periodontal ligaments.

stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes testing of cranial nerve reflexes. The examiner places a finger on the patient's chin and taps the finger downward with a reflex hammer. The patient demonstrates a brisk, hyperactive upward closure of the jaw (hyperactive jaw jerk reflex). Which type of motor neuron lesion does a hyperactive jaw jerk reflex indicate, and where is the lesion located?

options.text: Lower motor neuron lesion of CN V in the peripheral mandibular nerve
Lower motor neuron lesion of the trigeminal motor nucleus in the mid-pons
Bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion located rostral to the mid-pons
Unilateral lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII
Isolated spinal cord lesion at C5-C6

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion located rostral to the mid-pons.

The jaw jerk reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex mediated entirely by the mandibular nerve (CN V3):
• Afferent limb: Muscle spindle stretch travels via CN V3 to cell bodies in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus.
• Efferent limb: Direct monosynaptic synapse onto the trigeminal motor nucleus in the mid-pons → CN V3 → masseter contraction.
• Clinical significance: Under normal conditions, this reflex is minimal or absent. A brisk, hyperactive jaw jerk reflex is a pathognomonic sign of bilateral Upper Motor Neuron (pseudobulbar) pathology located above the mid-pons (such as in ALS or bilateral stroke), indicating that the lesion is intracranial and supranuclear.

stem: Pain and temperature sensation from the entire face enters the brainstem via the trigeminal nerve and descends in the spinal trigeminal tract to synapse in which specific subdivision of the spinal trigeminal nucleus, which extends caudally into the upper cervical spinal cord (C2-C3) and merges with the substantia gelatinosa?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Pars caudalis.

The spinal trigeminal nucleus is divided rostrocaudally into three subnuclei:
1. Pars oralis (rostral pons): Tactile and dental sensation.
2. Pars interpolaris (mid-medulla): Dental pain and tactile.
3. Pars caudalis (caudal medulla extending down to C2/C3 in the dorsal horn): The primary relay for pain and temperature from the head and face. Histologically continuous with the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord (Rexed lamina II), it sends crossed secondary axons (ventral trigeminothalamic tract) to the VPM nucleus of the thalamus.

stem: The three divisions of the trigeminal nerve exit the middle cranial fossa through three distinct skull base foramina. Which of the following lists correctly pairs the nerve division with its exit foramen?

options.text: V1: Superior orbital fissure; V2: Foramen rotundum; V3: Foramen ovale
V1: Optic canal; V2: Foramen ovale; V3: Foramen spinosum
V1: Foramen rotundum; V2: Superior orbital fissure; V3: Foramen lacerum
V1: Superior orbital fissure; V2: Foramen ovale; V3: Foramen rotundum
V1: Foramen ovale; V2: Foramen spinosum; V3: Jugular foramen

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. V1: Superior orbital fissure; V2: Foramen rotundum; V3: Foramen ovale.

Trigeminal skull foramina mnemonic ('Standing Room Only'):
• V1 (Ophthalmic): Superior orbital fissure (S)
• V2 (Maxillary): Foramen Rotundum (R)
• V3 (Mandibular): Foramen Ovale (O)

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with severe, burning pain and a vesicular erythematous rash over his right forehead, upper eyelid, and the tip and side of his nose (Hutchinson sign). Fluorescein staining reveals dendritic corneal ulcers. The presence of lesions on the tip of the nose indicates involvement of which specific nerve branch, placing the eye at high risk for vision loss?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Nasociliary nerve (external nasal branch).

This patient has Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion, V1 distribution). Hutchinson sign (vesicles on the tip, side, or root of the nose) indicates involvement of the external nasal branch of the nasociliary nerve. Because the nasociliary nerve also supplies sensory innervation to the cornea, ciliary body, and iris via long and short ciliary nerves, Hutchinson sign is a powerful clinical predictor of herpes zoster keratitis, uveitis, and potential blindness.

stem: The motor root of the trigeminal nerve travels exclusively with the mandibular division (CN V3). Which of the following muscles is innervated by the motor division of the trigeminal nerve?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Tensor tympani and mylohyoid.

Muscles innervated by the motor root of CN V3 (derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch):
• 4 Muscles of mastication: Masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid.
• Mylohyoid and anterior belly of the digastric.
• Tensor tympani (dampens sound of chewing on the malleus).
• Tensor veli palatini (tenses the soft palate).
(In contrast, facial expression muscles, stapedius, and posterior belly of the digastric are innervated by CN VII [2nd pharyngeal arch]).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent facial pain following dental surgery. Neuroimaging confirms compression of the trigeminal nerve. Sensory cell bodies for discriminative touch, pain, and temperature from the face (analogous to the dorsal root ganglion of spinal nerves) are located in which peripheral ganglion?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Trigeminal (Gasserian / semilunar) ganglion.

The trigeminal (semilunar or Gasserian) ganglion is located in Meckel cave, a dural recess on the petrous apex of the temporal bone in the middle cranial fossa. It contains pseudounipolar sensory cell bodies for almost all somatosensory modalities from the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve (V1, V2, V3). (The only exception is proprioception, whose cell bodies reside in the central mesencephalic nucleus).

stem: Discriminative fine touch and two-point discrimination from the facial skin and oral mucosa are relayed to which brainstem trigeminal nucleus, which is the cranial nerve analogue of the dorsal column nuclei (nucleus gracilis and cuneatus)?

options.text: Chief (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Chief (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.

The chief (principal) sensory nucleus of CN V is located in the mid-pons lateral to the trigeminal motor nucleus. It receives primary A-beta fibers conveying fine touch, pressure, and dental tactile sensation. Most second-order axons cross the midline and ascend in the ventral trigeminothalamic tract (trigeminal lemniscus) to the contralateral VPM nucleus of the thalamus (with a small uncrossed dorsal trigeminothalamic tract from oral structures).

stem: A 52-year-old man who experiences intractable trigeminal neuralgia refractory to carbamazepine and gabapentin undergoes microvascular decompression (Janetta procedure). During suboccipital craniectomy, which artery is most frequently identified as the compressive vessel impinging on the trigeminal nerve root?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Superior cerebellar artery (SCA).

In >75% of cases of classical trigeminal neuralgia, microvascular compression at the root entry zone (where the nerve transitions from central oligodendrocyte myelin to peripheral Schwann cell myelin) is caused by an aberrant, tortuous loop of the Superior Cerebellar Artery (SCA). Other culprits include the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) or a petrosal vein.

stem: Which of the following parasympathetic ganglia receives preganglionic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve and distributes postganglionic secretomotor fibers to the parotid salivary gland via the auriculotemporal branch of CN V3?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Otic ganglion.

Parasympathetic ganglia associated with branches of CN V ('COPS'):
• Ciliary (V1): CN III preganglionic → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves to pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
• Otic (V3): CN IX preganglionic (lesser petrosal) → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve (V3) to parotid gland.
• Pterygopalatine (V2): CN VII preganglionic (greater petrosal) → pterygopalatine ganglion → lacrimal gland, nasal/palatal glands.
• Submandibular (V3): CN VII preganglionic (chorda tympani) → lingual nerve (V3) → submandibular ganglion → submandibular and sublingual glands.

stem: During a routine dental procedure, an inferior alveolar nerve block is administered to anesthetize the mandibular teeth. This injection targets a nerve that is a branch of which division of the trigeminal nerve?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Mandibular division (V3).

The inferior alveolar nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It enters the mandibular foramen on the medial surface of the ramus, traverses the mandibular canal to provide sensory innervation to all lower teeth, and exits the mental foramen as the mental nerve (supplying sensation to the chin and lower lip).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with numbness of her right upper lip, right cheek, and upper teeth following a blow to the face that fractured the inferior orbital rim (orbital blowout fracture). Which specific nerve is compressed or injured as it courses through the floor of the orbit?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Infraorbital nerve.

In orbital blowout fractures (fracture of the thin orbital floor into the maxillary sinus), the infraorbital nerve (a direct continuation of the maxillary nerve CN V2) is frequently entrapped or contused as it traverses the infraorbital groove and canal in the orbital floor. This produces numbness, paresthesias, or hypesthesia of the ipsilateral lower eyelid, cheek, lateral nose, and upper lip/teeth.

stem: Ascending second-order fibers from the spinal trigeminal nucleus pars caudalis decussate across the brainstem midline and ascend to the VPM nucleus of the thalamus within which pathway?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Ventral trigeminothalamic tract (trigeminal lemniscus).

Second-order nociceptive and thermal axons from the spinal trigeminal nucleus pars caudalis cross the brainstem midline and ascend as the Ventral Trigeminothalamic Tract (VTHT), running adjacent to the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract. They terminate in the contralateral Ventral Posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus. (In contrast, the dorsal trigeminothalamic tract carries uncrossed fine touch from the principal sensory nucleus).

stem: Which of the following intracranial structures receives somatic sensory innervation from the tentorial nerve (recurrent meningeal branch of Arnold), derived from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1)?

options.text: Tentorium cerebelli and superior surface of the falx cerebri
Floor of the posterior cranial fossa around the foramen magnum
Middle ear ossicles and tympanic cavity
Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Tentorium cerebelli and superior surface of the falx cerebri.

Supratentorial dura mater (anterior and middle cranial fossae, anterior falx cerebri, and tentorium cerebelli) is innervated by the trigeminal nerve (principally CN V1 via the tentorial nerve of Arnold). Irritation or stretch of the tentorium (e.g., from posterior fossa tumors or subarachnoid blood) refers pain to the V1 distribution (forehead, retro-orbital area, and eyes). (In contrast, infratentorial dura in the posterior fossa is innervated by CN IX, CN X, and upper cervical nerves C1-C3, referring pain to the occiput and neck).

stem: On examination, when a patient is asked to open his mouth wide against resistance, the mandible deviates markedly to the right side. Strength of the left pterygoid muscles is normal. This finding localizes to a lower motor neuron lesion of which nerve?

options.text: Right trigeminal nerve motor root (CN V3)

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Right trigeminal nerve motor root (CN V3).

The lateral pterygoid muscle protrudes and depresses the mandible, pushing the chin toward the CONTRALATERAL side. When the right lateral pterygoid is paralyzed due to a right CN V3 LMN lesion, the unopposed action of the intact left lateral pterygoid muscle pushes the mandible toward the paralyzed (right) side upon opening ('the jaw deviates toward the side of the lesion').

stem: A 28-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presents with bilateral trigeminal neuralgia. Trigeminal neuralgia occurring bilaterally in a young patient is a classic presentation of which pathological process?

options.text: Demyelinating plaques within the intrapontine trigeminal primary afferent fibers

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Demyelinating plaques within the intrapontine trigeminal primary afferent fibers.

While classical trigeminal neuralgia in older adults is typically unilateral and caused by neurovascular compression, trigeminal neuralgia in young patients (<40 years old)—especially when BILATERAL—should immediately raise suspicion for Multiple Sclerosis. In MS, demyelinating plaques involve the central myelin (oligodendrocyte-myelinated) portion of the trigeminal root entry zone within the pons, causing ephaptic transmission.

stem: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1) divides into three major terminal branches before entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. Which of the following represents these three branches?

options.text: Greater petrosal, Lesser petrosal, and Deep petrosal nerves
Supraorbital, Supratrochlear, and Infratrochlear nerves only

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Frontal, Lacrimal, and Nasociliary nerves.

Branches of CN V1 mnemonic ('Football Lovers Need'):
• Frontal nerve (largest; divides into supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves to supply forehead and scalp).
• Lacrimal nerve (supplies lateral upper eyelid and conveys parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal gland).
• Nasociliary nerve (supplies cornea, ciliary body, ethmoid sinuses, and skin of nasal dorsum and tip via external nasal branch).

stem: In addition to conveying somatosensory fibers from the skin and mucous membranes of the face, cranial nerves VII, IX, and X also share the spinal trigeminal nucleus. Somatic sensory fibers from the external auditory canal and auricle traveling in the vagus nerve (Arnold nerve) synapse in which nucleus?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Spinal trigeminal nucleus.

All general somatic afferent (GSA) fibers from the head—regardless of whether they travel in CN V, CN VII (ear skin), CN IX (posterior ear canal and tympanic membrane), or CN X (auricular branch / Arnold nerve to external auditory canal)—converge and synapse in the Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus. This explains why stimulating the external ear canal with a cotton swab or ear speculum can trigger referred reflex coughing (vagal afferent converging with vagal autonomic motor pathways: the Arnold ear-cough reflex).

stem: A 25-year-old man with a family history of anesthetic complications undergoes emergency appendectomy. Anesthesia is induced with propofol and succinylcholine, followed by maintenance with inhaled sevoflurane. Within 15 minutes, his end-tidal CO2 rises sharply from 38 to 85 mm Hg despite hyperventilation. He develops generalized muscle rigidity, tachycardia (145 bpm), tachypnea, and his body temperature spikes to 41.2°C (106.2°F). Laboratory studies reveal severe metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia. Mutation in which gene is most commonly responsible for this life-threatening pharmacogenetic syndrome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. RYR1 (Ryanodine receptor 1).

This patient has Malignant Hyperthermia (MH):
• Trigger: Volatile halogenated inhaled anesthetics (sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane, halothane) or the depolarizing muscle relaxant Succinylcholine.
• Genetics: Autosomal dominant mutation in the RYR1 gene (~70-80% of cases) encoding the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor calcium release channel (or less commonly CACNA1S).
• Pathophysiology: Uncontrolled massive release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the myoplasm triggers sustained muscle contraction, hypermetabolism, ATP depletion, massive CO2 production, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and hyperkalemia.
• Treatment: Immediate discontinuation of triggers, hyperventilation with 100% O2, and IV Dantrolene.

stem: Dantrolene is the life-saving antidote for malignant hyperthermia. By what specific molecular mechanism does dantrolene arrest the hypermetabolic crisis of malignant hyperthermia?

options.text: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase to increase synaptic acetylcholine
Blocks ryanodine receptors (RYR1), preventing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Blocks ryanodine receptors (RYR1), preventing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Dantrolene is a skeletal muscle relaxant that acts intracellularly by directly binding to the Ryanodine Receptor 1 (RYR1) channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane. It inhibits channel opening, blocking the release of sequestered Ca2+ into the cytoplasm. This decouples excitation-contraction coupling, halting actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling and terminating the hypermetabolic cascade.

stem: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker commonly used for rapid sequence intubation. Following a single bolus of succinylcholine, a patient exhibits Phase I neuromuscular blockade. Which of the following electrophysiological findings on train-of-four (TOF) peripheral nerve stimulation is characteristic of Phase I block?

options.text: Constant but equal reduction in twitch height across all four stimuli (no fade) and absent post-tetanic potentiation
Progressive decrease in twitch height across the four stimuli (fade) with post-tetanic facilitation
Complete reversal of the block following administration of neostigmine
Selective enhancement of the fourth twitch relative to the first
Complete absence of motor endplate depolarization

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Constant but equal reduction in twitch height across all four stimuli (no fade) and absent post-tetanic potentiation.

Comparison of Neuromuscular Blockade Phases:
• Phase I Block (depolarizing block by succinylcholine): Sustained depolarization of the motor endplate. On Train-of-Four (TOF), all 4 twitches are equally reduced in amplitude (NO fade, TOF ratio = 1.0). There is NO post-tetanic facilitation. Reversal by neostigmine is CONTRAINDICATED (it intensifies Phase I block by inhibiting butyrylcholinesterase).
• Phase II Block (desensitization block from prolonged/repeated succinylcholine exposure or non-depolarizing agents): Characterized by FADE on TOF (progressive decrease in twitch height 1 to 4) and post-tetanic facilitation; CAN be reversed by neostigmine.

stem: A 30-year-old man who sustained full-thickness third-degree burns covering 45% of his body surface area 10 days ago requires emergency surgical debridement. The anesthesiologist avoids using succinylcholine for intubation. Why is succinylcholine strictly contraindicated in patients with severe burns, crush injuries, or denervation injuries?

options.text: Risk of severe hypocalcemia and tetany
Risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia and fatal cardiac arrest
Immediate metabolism by pseudocholinesterase rendering it ineffective
Risk of severe hypertension and cerebral hemorrhage

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia and fatal cardiac arrest.

In severe burns, crush injuries, stroke, or denervation injuries, skeletal muscle undergoes widespread upregulation and proliferation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors (including embryonic alpha-7 nicotinic AChRs) across the entire sarcolemma. Administration of succinylcholine causes open-channel depolarization across these vast extrajunctional receptors, resulting in massive, uncontrolled efflux of intracellular K+ into the circulation. Serum potassium can surge by 5-10 mEq/L within minutes, triggering ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.

stem: A 24-year-old woman undergoes elective laparoscopic surgery. She receives succinylcholine for tracheal intubation. Normally, muscle paralysis from succinylcholine resolves within 5 to 10 minutes. However, this patient remains completely paralyzed and apneic for over 4 hours postoperatively. Which genetic enzyme deficiency is the cause of her prolonged neuromuscular blockade?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase / plasma cholinesterase) deficiency.

Succinylcholine is normally rapidly hydrolyzed in the bloodstream by plasma Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase / BCHE), synthesized by the liver, giving it a brief clinical duration of 5-10 minutes. Patients with atypical or deficient pseudocholinesterase (autosomal recessive inheritance, detected by the dibucaine number test) cannot metabolize succinylcholine, leading to persistent neuromuscular blockade and prolonged apnea lasting several hours. Management is mechanical ventilation until the drug clears passively.

stem: The potency of an inhaled general anesthetic is quantified by its Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC). Agent X has a MAC of 1.2%, while Agent Y has a MAC of 6.0%. Which of the following statements comparing these two anesthetics is correct?

options.text: Agent Y is 5 times more potent than Agent X
Agent X is 5 times more potent than Agent Y
Agent X induces anesthesia faster than Agent Y
Agent Y has a higher oil-gas partition coefficient than Agent X
Agent X and Agent Y have equal potency

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Agent X is 5 times more potent than Agent Y.

• Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) is the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic at 1 atmosphere of pressure that prevents movement in 50% of patients in response to a standard surgical incision (noxious stimulus).
• MAC is INVERSELY proportional to potency (Potency = 1 / MAC).
• Agent X (MAC 1.2%) has a lower MAC than Agent Y (MAC 6.0%), meaning Agent X requires a lower concentration to produce anesthesia and is therefore 5 times more potent (6.0 / 1.2 = 5).
• Potency correlates directly with lipid solubility (high oil-gas partition coefficient / Meyer-Overton rule).

stem: The speed of induction and recovery of an inhaled general anesthetic is primarily determined by which physicochemical property?

options.text: Molecular weight of the anesthetic molecule

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Blood-gas partition coefficient (solubility in blood).

• Speed of induction/recovery is INVERSELY proportional to blood solubility (blood-gas partition coefficient):
  - Insoluble gases (low blood-gas coefficient, e.g., nitrous oxide = 0.47, desflurane = 0.42): Very little gas dissolves in blood; blood saturates quickly, allowing alveolar and arterial partial pressures to rise rapidly, which rapidly equilibrates with brain partial pressure → FAST induction and FAST recovery.
  - Highly soluble gases (high blood-gas coefficient, e.g., halothane = 2.4): Large amounts of drug dissolve in blood (acting as a sponge); alveolar and arterial partial pressures rise slowly → SLOW induction and SLOW recovery.

stem: Which intravenous anesthetic is an alkylphenol derivative that potentiates GABA-A receptors, causes rapid onset of anesthesia with smooth recovery, possesses significant antiemetic properties, but can cause vasodilation, hypotension, and 'propofol infusion syndrome' during prolonged high-dose infusions?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Propofol.

Propofol (2,6-diisopropylphenol) is the most widely used IV induction agent:
• Mechanism: Allosteric potentiation of inhibitory GABA-A receptors and direct channel gating at higher concentrations.
• Clinical advantages: Rapid onset (~30-40 seconds), rapid emergence, and intrinsic antiemetic properties.
• Adverse effects: Marked systemic vasodilation and myocardial depression (hypotension). Prolonged high-dose ICU infusion can cause Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS: metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, hyperlipidemia, rhabdomyolysis, hepatomegaly, and refractory heart failure).

stem: A 75-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis and ischemic cardiomyopathy requires emergency abdominal surgery. The anesthesiologist selects etomidate for induction because of its remarkable hemodynamic stability. What is the major endocrine adverse effect of etomidate that limits its use to single induction boluses?

options.text: Inhibition of insulin release causing severe ketoacidosis
Inhibition of 11-beta-hydroxylase causing primary adrenocortical suppression
Suppression of parathyroid hormone causing tetany
Stimulation of antidiuretic hormone causing severe hyponatremia

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Inhibition of 11-beta-hydroxylase causing primary adrenocortical suppression.

Etomidate is an imidazole-derived IV induction agent prized for its minimal cardiovascular depression (no drop in blood pressure or cardiac output). However, its imidazole ring binds to and inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, the key enzyme converting 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol (and 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone) in the adrenal cortex. Even a single induction dose can cause transient primary adrenal insufficiency, and continuous infusions are associated with increased mortality in septic shock.

stem: A 10-year-old child with severe asthma requires closed reduction of a fractured forearm in the emergency department. Ketamine is administered. Ketamine provides 'dissociative anesthesia' where the patient appears awake with eyes open but is completely detached from the environment. What is the primary molecular mechanism of action of ketamine?

options.text: Non-competitive antagonist at NMDA glutamate receptors

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Non-competitive antagonist at NMDA glutamate receptors.

Ketamine (a phencyclidine / PCP derivative) acts as a non-competitive antagonist at the NMDA receptor ion channel pore, inhibiting excitatory glutamatergic transmission in the cortex and limbic system:
• Effects: Dissociative anesthesia, intense analgesia, and amnesia, while preserving spontaneous respiration and airway reflexes.
• Sympathomimetic: Inhibits catecholamine reuptake, increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and causing bronchodilation (ideal for asthmatics and hypovolemic trauma patients).
• Adverse effects: Increases intracranial pressure (ICP) and causes emergence delirium/vivid hallucinations (reduced by co-administering benzodiazepines).

stem: Which of the following intravenous sedative-anesthetics is a highly selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that acts in the locus coeruleus to produce conscious sedation that resembles natural non-REM sleep, provides mild analgesia, and does not cause respiratory depression?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Dexmedetomidine.

Dexmedetomidine is a potent, centrally-acting alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist (selectivity ratio alpha-2:alpha-1 is 1620:1, ~8x higher than clonidine):
• Mechanism: Binds presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the locus coeruleus of the pons, inhibiting norepinephrine release.
• Unique features: Produces 'cooperative sedation' (patients are easily rousable and can follow commands when stimulated) without causing respiratory depression, making it ideal for ICU weaning from mechanical ventilation and awake fiberoptic intubation.
• Side effects: Bradycardia and hypotension.

stem: Which non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drug is an isoquinoline derivative that undergoes spontaneous, non-enzymatic degradation in plasma and tissue via Hofmann elimination at physiological body temperature and pH, making it the neuromuscular blocker of choice for patients with renal or hepatic failure?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Cisatracurium (and atracurium).

Cisatracurium and atracurium are benzylisoquinolinium non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers that undergo organ-independent elimination:
• Hofmann elimination: Spontaneous chemical breakdown of the molecule in plasma and tissues driven purely by physiological pH (7.4) and temperature (37°C) into inactive laudanosine and monoquaternary alcohol.
• Because clearance does not depend on liver metabolism or renal excretion, cisatracurium is the preferred paralytic agent for patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or severe hepatic failure, and for prolonged neuromuscular blockade in ARDS.

stem: During a knee arthroscopy under local infiltration anesthesia, 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine is inadvertently injected into a vein. Five minutes later, the patient develops circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste in his mouth, followed immediately by generalized tonic-clonic seizures, severe bradycardia, wide-complex ventricular tachycardia, and cardiovascular collapse. Which of the following is the specific rescue antidote for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Intravenous 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid).

This patient has Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST):
• Bupivacaine is highly lipophilic and dissociates very slowly from cardiac sodium channels during diastole ('fast in, slow out'), leading to severe cardiotoxicity, refractory ventricular arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest.
• Antidote: 20% IV Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid). Mechanism involves the 'lipid sink' theory (the lipid emulsion creates an intravascular lipid phase that sequesters the lipophilic bupivacaine away from target tissues in the heart and brain) and direct metabolic/inotropic support to cardiac mitochondria.

stem: Local anesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels from the intracellular side of the axonal membrane. To reach their binding site, local anesthetics must cross the lipophilic lipid bilayer in which chemical form, and bind to the channel in which chemical form?

options.text: Cross membrane as ionized (charged); bind to channel as non-ionized (uncharged)
Cross membrane as non-ionized (uncharged/base); bind to channel as ionized (charged/cation)
Cross membrane as ionized; bind to channel as ionized
Cross membrane as non-ionized; bind to channel as non-ionized

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cross membrane as non-ionized (uncharged/base); bind to channel as ionized (charged/cation).

Local anesthetics are weak bases (pKa typically 7.6-8.9):
• To diffuse across the hydrophobic neuronal lipid bilayer, the molecule MUST be in its uncharged (non-ionized, free base) form (B).
• Once inside the axoplasm, the molecule becomes protonated into its charged, ionized cation form (BH+).
• The ionized (BH+) form binds to the intracellular mouth of the voltage-gated Na+ channel to block Na+ conductance.
• In infected or inflamed tissue (acidic pH < 6.0), more of the drug is ionized outside the cell, preventing membrane penetration and explaining why local anesthetics are ineffective in abscesses.

stem: Which of the following inhaled anesthetics has the lowest blood-gas partition coefficient (0.42), allowing the fastest induction and emergence of all volatile agents, but can cause airway irritation, coughing, and breath-holding during inhalation induction, requiring a specialized heated vaporizer?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Desflurane.

• Desflurane has the lowest blood-gas solubility (0.42) of all volatile agents, providing near-instantaneous changes in anesthetic depth and rapid emergence regardless of procedure duration.
• However, it has a high vapor pressure (boils at 22.8°C / room temperature), requiring a specialized heated, pressurized vaporizer (Tec 6).
• It is pungent and irritates the airway, making it unsuitable for mask induction.
• (In contrast, Sevoflurane has sweet, non-pungent odor and is preferred for pediatric mask induction).

stem: A 58-year-old woman undergoes elective surgery with halothane anesthesia in a developing country. Five days postoperatively, she develops anorexia, nausea, fever, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals marked AST and ALT elevations (>3,000 U/L) and a prolonged prothrombin time. Liver biopsy shows massive centrilobular hepatic necrosis. What is the pathogenesis of halothane hepatitis?

options.text: Direct dose-dependent toxic inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation
Immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction against trifluoroacetylated liver proteins
Biliary sludge obstruction of the common bile duct
Ischemic necrosis from portal vein thrombosis

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction against trifluoroacetylated liver proteins.

Halothane undergoes significant hepatic metabolism (~20-25%) by CYP2E1, producing a reactive trifluoroacetyl (TFA) chloride intermediate. This intermediate covalently binds to normal hepatocyte proteins, forming trifluoroacetylated neoantigens. In susceptible patients (especially with prior halothane exposure), the immune system generates anti-TFA antibodies that trigger a severe, antibody-mediated auto-allergic response, causing fulminant centrilobular hepatic necrosis (halothane hepatitis) with a mortality rate of up to 50%.

stem: Which of the following local anesthetics is formulated with prilocaine in EMLA cream, can be used for mucous membrane anesthesia, and can cause methemoglobinemia (chocolate-colored blood and cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen) as a classic toxic metabolite adverse effect?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Benzocaine (and Prilocaine).

Benzocaine (topical spray for endoscopy/dental work) and Prilocaine (metabolized to o-toluidine) can oxidize ferrous iron (Fe2+) in hemoglobin to ferric iron (Fe3+), forming Methemoglobin. Methemoglobin cannot bind oxygen and shifts the remaining hemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve to the left (tissue hypoxia). Patients present with 'chocolate brown' blood, cyanosis, and low oxygen saturation (pulse oximeter reads ~85% regardless of actual PO2). Treatment: IV Methylene Blue (reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+).

stem: Why is epinephrine frequently added to local anesthetic solutions (e.g., 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine) for infiltration into peripheral tissues?

options.text: To increase the systemic absorption of the local anesthetic
To induce local vasoconstriction, which prolongs the duration of anesthesia and decreases systemic toxicity
To decrease the latency of local anesthetic onset by neutralizing tissue pH
To directly block voltage-gated sodium channels
To prevent allergic reactions to ester local anesthetics

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. To induce local vasoconstriction, which prolongs the duration of anesthesia and decreases systemic toxicity.

Epinephrine acts on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in local vascular smooth muscle, causing profound vasoconstriction. This:
1. Decreases local blood flow, reducing surgical bleeding.
2. Slows systemic absorption of the local anesthetic into the bloodstream, prolonging the local duration of action.
3. Decreases peak plasma concentrations of the local anesthetic, lowering the risk of systemic toxicity (LAST).

stem: Which of the following competitive non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents has the most rapid onset of action (60–90 seconds at a dose of 1.2 mg/kg), making it the primary non-depolarizing alternative to succinylcholine for rapid sequence intubation (RSI)?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Rocuronium.

Rocuronium is an aminosteroid non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Because it has relatively low potency compared to vecuronium, a larger molar dose is administered. This high concentration gradient drives rapid diffusion to the neuromuscular junction, providing intubating conditions in 60-90 seconds. It is the primary non-depolarizing drug for Rapid Sequence Intubation when succinylcholine is contraindicated (burns, hyperkalemia, denervation). Its effects can be rapidly reversed by sugammadex.

stem: Which of the following intravenous general anesthetics is an ultra-short-acting barbiturate that induces anesthesia within one arm-brain circulation time (~20 seconds) and whose rapid recovery from a single bolus is driven not by metabolic clearance, but by rapid redistribution from the brain to skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Thiopental.

Thiopental is an ultra-short-acting barbiturate with high lipid solubility:
• Onset: Crosses the blood-brain barrier rapidly into the well-perfused brain within 20-30 seconds.
• Termination of action: Patient awakens within 5-10 minutes following a single bolus dose. This termination is NOT due to hepatic metabolism, but rather rapid REDISTRIBUTION of the drug from highly perfused organs (brain, heart) to intermediate-perfused tissues (skeletal muscle) and ultimately into poorly perfused adipose tissue.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent, severe, throbbing headaches that are strictly unilateral (left-sided) and last 12 to 24 hours. During attacks, she experiences nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to bright light (photophobia) and loud sounds (phonophobia). Prior to headache onset, she sees shimmering, jagged, zigzag lines with a blind spot in her right visual field lasting 30 minutes. What underlying neurophysiological process is responsible for the visual aura in migraine?

options.text: Acute spasm of the ophthalmic artery causing retinal ischemia
Transient occlusion of the basilar artery

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cortical spreading depression (CSD).

Migraine with aura is mediated by Cortical Spreading Depression (CSD):
• A self-propagating wave of slow cellular depolarization (traveling at 2-5 mm/min across the cerebral cortex, typically occipital), followed by prolonged neuronal and glial suppression.
• The initial wave of depolarization triggers visual scintillating scotomas (aura), while the subsequent activation of meningeal trigeminal perivascular nerves stimulates the release of pro-inflammatory neuropeptides (CGRP, substance P), causing neurogenic vasodilation and throbbing headache.

stem: Sumatriptan is an acute abortive medication for moderate-to-severe migraine attacks. Sumatriptan provides rapid relief by acting as an agonist at which specific serotonin receptor subtypes?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors.

Triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) are selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists:
• 5-HT1B receptors: Located on intracranial and meningeal blood vessels; activation causes vasoconstriction of painfully dilated cerebral vessels.
• 5-HT1D receptors: Located presynaptically on trigeminal nerve endings; activation inhibits the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P, suppressing neurogenic inflammation and central pain transmission.
• Contraindication: Coronary artery disease or Prinzmetal angina (can cause coronary vasospasm).

stem: A 35-year-old male smoker awakens at 2:00 AM every night for the past 2 weeks with excruciating, piercing, 'ice-pick' pain centered behind his right eye. The pain lasts 45 minutes and is accompanied by ipsilateral eye redness, profuse tearing (lacrimation), nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and partial ptosis with miosis (Horner syndrome). During attacks, he paces around the room agitated and unable to lie still. What is the most effective first-line acute abortive treatment for this condition?

options.text: 100% high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask and subcutaneous sumatriptan

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. 100% high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask and subcutaneous sumatriptan.

This patient has Cluster Headache (a Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia / TAC):
• Clinical hallmarks: Strictly unilateral, severe retro-orbital/temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, nocturnal predilection, ipsilateral autonomic signs (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, Horner syndrome), and motor restlessness/pacing.
• Acute abortive treatment: 100% High-flow Oxygen (12-15 L/min via non-rebreather mask) is first-line and highly effective within 10-15 minutes; subcutaneous sumatriptan or zolmitriptan nasal spray are also first-line.
• Prophylaxis: Verapamil is the first-line preventive drug of choice.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with severe right-sided temple headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, malaise, and fatigue. For the past month, she has experienced pain and fatigue in her jaw when chewing tough meats (jaw claudication). She also complains of bilateral aching and morning stiffness in her shoulders and hips. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 105 mm/hr and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 45 mg/L. What is the most feared complication if treatment is delayed, and what is the immediate management?

options.text: Rupture of a cerebral aneurysm; Urgent neurosurgical clipping
Irreversible blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; Immediate high-dose oral prednisone

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Irreversible blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; Immediate high-dose oral prednisone.

This patient has Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis (GCA), commonly associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica:
• Presentation: Age >50, new unaccustomed headache, temporal artery tenderness/induration, jaw claudication (highly specific), and markedly elevated ESR/CRP.
• Feared complication: Permanent, irreversible blindness due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head (Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy / AION).
• Management: Immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 60 mg/day or IV methylprednisolone if visual symptoms exist) MUST be initiated immediately before waiting for a temporal artery biopsy (which demonstrates granulomatous inflammation of the media with multinucleated giant cells).

stem: A 45-year-old accountant presents with a dull, bilateral, aching headache that feels like a 'tight band squeezing around my entire head.' The headache is present almost daily, worsening toward the end of the workday. There is no nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia, and physical activity does not worsen the pain. Examination reveals pericranial muscle tenderness upon palpation of the trapezius and temporalis muscles. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Tension-type headache.

Tension-type headache (TTH) is the most common primary headache disorder in adults:
• Clinical features: Bilateral, non-pulsatile, dull/pressing/tightening pain ('tight band or vise around the head'), mild-to-moderate intensity, not aggravated by routine physical activity.
• Diagnostic criteria: NO nausea or vomiting; at most one of photophobia OR phonophobia (never both).
• Physical exam: Tenderness of pericranial and neck/shoulder musculature.
• Acute treatment: NSAIDs, acetaminophen, aspirin.
• Chronic prophylaxis (if >15 days/month): Amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant).

stem: Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) is a 37-amino acid neuropeptide that plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of migraine by inducing potent intracranial vasodilation and mast cell degranulation. Which of the following monoclonal antibodies is approved for migraine prevention and acts by specifically binding to and blocking the CGRP receptor?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Erenumab.

CGRP-targeted therapies for migraine:
• CGRP Receptor antagonist monoclonal antibody: Erenumab (specifically binds to the canonical CGRP receptor complex).
• CGRP Ligand-targeted monoclonal antibodies: Fremanezumab, Galcanezumab, and Eptinezumab (bind directly to the circulating CGRP peptide itself).
• Small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists ('gepants'): Ubrogepant, Rimegepant, and Atogepant (oral agents for acute treatment and/or prevention).
