stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of episodic migraines presents with daily, dull, diffuse headaches that have worsened over the past 4 months. She reports taking combination acetaminophen/aspirin/caffeine tablets 5 days a week, plus rizatriptan 3 to 4 days a week for the last 6 months. Whenever she tries to stop taking these medications, her headache intensifies severely within 24 hours. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Medication overuse headache (rebound headache).

Medication Overuse Headache (MOH) occurs in patients with pre-existing primary headache disorders (usually migraine):
• Diagnostic criteria: Headache present on ≥15 days per month in a patient with regular overuse of acute headache medications for >3 months (≥10 days/month for triptans, opioids, or combination analgesics; ≥15 days/month for simple NSAIDs/acetaminophen).
• Presentation: Daily, dull, refractory headache present upon waking that temporarily abates after taking analgesics, only to recur when the drug wears off.
• Treatment: Complete withdrawal of the overused acute medication, bridging therapy, and initiation of a preventive medication (e.g., topiramate, beta-blocker, or CGRP antibody).

stem: A 30-year-old woman with frequent disabling migraines is evaluated for preventive therapy. Which of the following oral medications is an anticonvulsant approved for migraine prophylaxis that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, potentiates GABA, inhibits AMPA receptors, and commonly causes paresthesias, weight loss, kidney stones, and cognitive slowing ('dopamax')?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Topiramate.

Topiramate is a first-line oral preventive agent for chronic and high-frequency episodic migraine:
• Multiple mechanisms: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, potentiates GABA-A receptor currents, inhibits AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors, and weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase.
• Side effect profile: Paresthesias (distal tingling due to carbonic anhydrase inhibition), anorexia and weight loss (often favored by patients), nephrolithiasis (calcium phosphate stones), metabolic acidosis, and word-finding difficulty/cognitive blunting ('dopamax'). It is also teratogenic (cleft lip/palate).

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with severe unilateral retro-orbital headaches that recur 10 to 20 times per day, each lasting 15 to 30 minutes, accompanied by prominent ipsilateral conjunctival injection and rhinorrhea. Brain MRI is normal. The attacks completely resolve within 48 hours of starting indomethacin. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Paroxysmal hemicrania.

Paroxysmal Hemicrania is a Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC) that predominantly affects women:
• Clinical presentation: Frequent (usually >5 per day, up to 30/day), brief (2-30 minutes), excruciating unilateral retro-orbital pain accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features.
• Hallmark: Complete, absolute responsiveness to therapeutic doses of INDOMETHACIN (indomethacin-responsive headache). If a patient fails to respond to indomethacin, the diagnosis is excluded.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with migraine attacks fails therapy with triptans because of severe chest tightness and palpitations. She has a history of coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina). The physician prescribes lasmiditan. Lasmiditan aborts acute migraine attacks without causing vasoconstriction by selectively activating which serotonin receptor?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. 5-HT1F receptor.

Lasmiditan is a selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist ('ditan'):
• Unlike triptans (which bind 5-HT1B and cause vasoconstriction), 5-HT1F receptors are located exclusively on trigeminal sensory neurons and in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis without vascular expression.
• Activation inhibits trigeminal neuropeptide release and central pain transmission without causing vasoconstriction.
• It is safe in patients with coronary artery disease, stroke, or peripheral vascular disease (though it causes central sedation).

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with episodic headaches. His attacks are strictly unilateral, last 2 to 3 hours, and are triggered predictably within 1 hour of consuming a single alcoholic drink during cluster periods. Verapamil is prescribed for prevention. Verapamil prevents cluster headaches primarily through which pharmacological mechanism?

options.text: Potentiation of GABA-A receptors in the hypothalamus
Blockade of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels modulating hypothalamic-trigeminal circuitry
Competitive inhibition of beta-1 adrenergic receptors
Inhibition of neuronal nitric oxide synthase

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Blockade of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels modulating hypothalamic-trigeminal circuitry.

Verapamil (a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) is the first-line prophylactic medication for cluster headache:
• It blocks L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle and central neurons, stabilizing the posterior hypothalamic pacemaker and inhibiting trigeminovascular activation.
• High doses are often required (240-960 mg/day), necessitating baseline and surveillance ECGs to monitor for PR interval prolongation and heart block.

stem: Which brain structure acts as the primary 'biological clock' and generator for the circadian rhythmicity and nocturnal clustering seen in cluster headaches?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Posterior hypothalamus (suprachiasmatic nucleus circuitry).

Cluster headache is closely linked to hypothalamic dysfunction:
• Attacks demonstrate striking circadian periodicity (frequently striking at the exact same hour every night during REM sleep) and circannual periodicity (clustering in spring and autumn).
• Functional PET and fMRI imaging show selective activation of the ipsilateral posterior hypothalamic gray matter during acute cluster attacks, confirming the hypothalamus as the central generator.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the student health clinic with a throbbing unilateral headache accompanied by photophobia. She has asthma. Which of the following first-line migraine prophylactic medications should be avoided in this patient because of the risk of life-threatening bronchospasm?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Propranolol.

Propranolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist (blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors) approved as first-line migraine prophylaxis. Because it blocks beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, it prevents endogenous epinephrine-mediated bronchodilation and can precipitate severe bronchospasm in patients with asthma or COPD. In asthmatic migraineurs, topiramate, valproate, or CGRP monoclonal antibodies are preferred.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with chronic migraine (>15 headache days per month for >3 months, with at least 8 meeting migraine criteria) fails multiple oral prophylactic medications. Which treatment involves injecting a neurotoxin into 31 specific sites across the forehead, temples, back of the head, and neck every 12 weeks to prevent chronic migraine?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox).

OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) is FDA-approved for the prophylaxis of Chronic Migraine (headache ≥15 days/month, with ≥8 days meeting migraine criteria):
• Administration: 155 units divided across 31 standardized pericranial injection sites (corrugator, procerus, frontalis, temporalis, occipitalis, cervical paraspinal, and trapezius muscles) every 12 weeks.
• Mechanism: Cleaves SNAP-25 in peripheral nociceptive nerve endings, inhibiting the release of glutamate, substance P, and CGRP, thereby reducing peripheral nociceptive input to the trigeminal nucleus caudalis and preventing central sensitization.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with severe episodic headaches preceded by vertigo, bilateral tinnitus, dysarthria, diplopia, and ataxia lasting 45 minutes, followed by an intense occipital throbbing headache. Motor strength is completely normal, and brain MRI is unremarkable. What specific subtype of migraine with aura is present?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Migraine with brainstem aura (basilar-type migraine).

Migraine with Brainstem Aura (formerly basilar migraine):
• Clinical criteria: Migraine accompanied by aura symptoms originating clearly from the brainstem (dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, hyperacusis, diplopia, bilateral ataxia, decreased level of consciousness) without motor weakness.
• Triptans and ergotamines are historically avoided in this disorder due to theoretical concerns over basilar artery vasoconstriction.

stem: Familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM) is a rare autosomal dominant form of migraine with aura characterized by reversible motor weakness during the aura phase. FHM type 1 is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the CACNA1A gene on chromosome 19p13. What ion channel is encoded by CACNA1A?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel (Cav2.1).

Familial Hemiplegic Migraine (FHM) genetics:
• FHM1 (~50% of cases): Mutations in CACNA1A encoding the pore-forming alpha-1A subunit of neuronal P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cav2.1). (Also causes episodic ataxia type 2 and spinocerebellar ataxia type 6).
• FHM2: Mutations in ATP1A2 encoding the alpha-2 subunit of Na+/K+ ATPase.
• FHM3: Mutations in SCN1A encoding the voltage-gated Na+ channel Nav1.1.
These channelopathies increase cortical glutamate release, lowering the threshold for cortical spreading depression.

stem: Which of the following classes of acute migraine medications includes dihydroergotamine (DHE) and ergotamine tartrate, which act as non-selective agonists at multiple 5-HT, dopamine, and alpha-adrenergic receptors, and are strictly contraindicated in pregnant patients due to their potent oxytocic uterine-stimulating properties?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Ergot alkaloids.

Ergot alkaloids (ergotamine, dihydroergotamine / DHE) are derived from the fungus Claviceps purpurea:
• Broad pharmacology: Non-selective agonists at 5-HT1, 5-HT2, alpha-1, alpha-2, and dopamine receptors, producing prolonged vasoconstriction.
• Adverse effects: Nausea (dopaminergic CTZ stimulation), coronary vasospasm, and peripheral gangrene ('ergotism' / St. Anthony's fire).
• Contraindication: Pregnancy (causes uterine smooth muscle contraction and fetal abortion) and uncontrolled hypertension / vascular disease.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a severe migraine attack lasting 4 days that has failed oral sumatriptan and ketorolac (status migrainosus). In addition to IV fluids and IV ketorolac, which IV antiemetic dopamine D2 antagonist is commonly administered to provide both antiemetic and acute abortive analgesic relief?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Metoclopramide (or Prochlorperazine).

In status migrainosus (migraine lasting >72 hours), IV dopamine receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or chlorpromazine) are first-line therapies in the emergency department:
• Mechanisms: Block D2 receptors in the area postrema to relieve nausea and vomiting, and modulate central trigeminovascular processing to provide significant headache relief.
• Co-administration: Diphenhydramine is often co-administered to prevent acute dystonic extrapyramidal reactions and akathisia.

stem: Which of the following 'red flag' headache clinical features is captured by the mnemonic SNOOP and warrants immediate emergency neuroimaging (CT or MRI) to rule out life-threatening secondary headache disorders?

options.text: Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), Neurologic deficits, Onset sudden (thunderclap), Older age (>50), Pattern change / Positional
Stress, Nausea, Occipital location, Oral contraceptive use, Photophobia
Sinus congestion, Neck stiffness only, Ocular itching, Paresthesias in fingertips
Sleep deprivation, Nocturnal awakening, Ophthalmic aura, Pulsatile pain
Subacute onset, Nasal discharge, Osmophobia, Pain relieved by sleep

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), Neurologic deficits, Onset sudden (thunderclap), Older age (>50), Pattern change / Positional.

The SNOOP mnemonic for secondary headache red flags:
• S: Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, HIV, cancer) or Secondary risk factors
• N: Neurologic symptoms or abnormal signs (confusion, focal deficit, papilledema)
• O: Onset sudden (thunderclap / maximal in seconds: rule out SAH)
• O: Older age at onset (>50 years: rule out giant cell arteritis or mass)
• P: Pattern change, Positional worsening (rule out intracranial hypo/hypertension), Precipitated by Valsalva/cough, or Papilledema.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with persistent, strictly unilateral continuous headache present for 8 months without pain-free periods (hemicrania continua). She experiences superimposed exacerbations with ipsilateral eye tearing and ptosis. Brain MRI is normal. What pharmacological challenge confirms the diagnosis of hemicrania continua?

options.text: Complete, dramatic relief with oral indomethacin
Improvement following a trial of sumatriptan

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Complete, dramatic relief with oral indomethacin.

Hemicrania Continua is a primary headache disorder characterized by continuous, strictly unilateral, daily headache for >3 months with fluctuating intensity and autonomic features. By diagnostic criteria, it is universally and completely responsive to INDOMETHACIN. An 'indomethacin challenge' (indotest) confirms the diagnosis.

stem: A 23-year-old college student presents to the emergency department with acute intoxication after ingesting a high-dose cannabis edible. Physical examination reveals bilateral conjunctival injection, dry oral mucosa, resting tachycardia (heart rate 118 bpm), orthostatic lightheadedness, and increased appetite ('the munchies'). Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) produces these psychoactive and physiological manifestations primarily by acting as a partial agonist at which receptor subtype?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1).

Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the primary psychoactive cannabinoid in marijuana:
• Receptors: THC acts as a partial agonist at CB1 receptors (predominantly localized in the CNS—cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and hypothalamic appetite centers) and CB2 receptors (primarily on peripheral immune cells and lymphoid tissues).
• Signaling: CB1 is a Gi/o-protein coupled receptor that inhibits adenylyl cyclase, closes presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and opens inwardly rectifying K+ channels, decreasing presynaptic release of GABA and glutamate.
• Acute physiological signs: Bilateral conjunctival injection (ciliary vasodilation), tachycardia, dry mouth, increased appetite, and impaired short-term memory.

stem: A 26-year-old man with a 6-year history of heavy, daily cannabis use presents with recurrent episodes of intractable nausea, cyclic vomiting, and severe diffuse abdominal pain over the past 3 months. Extensive gastrointestinal workup, including upper endoscopy, abdominal CT, and gastric emptying studies, is completely normal. The patient notes that his nausea and pain are temporarily relieved only when he takes prolonged, extremely hot showers or baths multiple times a day. What is the diagnosis, and what is the definitive cure?

options.text: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS); Complete cessation of cannabis

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS); Complete cessation of cannabis.

Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS) occurs in chronic, heavy, long-term cannabis users:
• Clinical triad: Severe cyclic vomiting, colicky abdominal pain, and learned compulsive hot water bathing/showering (which transiently alleviates symptoms).
• Pathophysiology: Chronic overstimulation causes downregulation of central CB1 receptors and paradoxical pro-emetic effects, as well as desensitization of peripheral enteric TRPV1 heat-sensitive channels (hot water activates cutaneous TRPV1 to restore thermoregulatory and visceral balance).
• Acute relief: Topical capsaicin cream applied to the abdomen or IV haloperidol.
• Definitive cure: Permanent cessation of all cannabis consumption.

stem: A 29-year-old daily cannabis user abruptly discontinues marijuana use before starting a new job. Three days later, he presents with irritability, marked anxiety, insomnia, vivid disturbing dreams, tremors, sweating, and decreased appetite with weight loss. What condition is this patient experiencing, and at what time point do these symptoms typically peak?

options.text: Cannabis withdrawal syndrome; Peaks at 2 to 6 days
Panic disorder; Peaks immediately upon cessation

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cannabis withdrawal syndrome; Peaks at 2 to 6 days.

Cannabis Withdrawal Syndrome (DSM-5 criteria):
• Onset: Symptoms develop within 24-48 hours of cessation in heavy, daily users.
• Symptoms: Irritability, anger/aggression, nervousness/anxiety, sleep disturbance (insomnia, vivid strange dreams), decreased appetite/weight loss, restlessness, depressed mood, and physical symptoms (tremors, sweating, chills, headache).
• Time course: Symptoms typically peak at 2 to 6 days after stopping and gradually resolve over 1 to 2 weeks as lipophilic cannabinoids clear the body.

stem: Endocannabinoids act as unconventional retrograde neurotransmitters in the central nervous system. Which of the following molecules is an endogenous lipid-derived cannabinoid that is synthesized 'on demand' from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase D and acts as an agonist at CB1 and CB2 receptors?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Anandamide (N-arachidonoylethanolamine).

The two primary endogenous cannabinoids (endocannabinoids) are:
1. Anandamide (AEA / N-arachidonoylethanolamine, derived from N-arachidonoyl phosphatidylethanolamine).
2. 2-Arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG, synthesized from diacylglycerol by DAG lipase).
Endocannabinoids are not stored in vesicles; upon postsynaptic depolarization and Ca2+ influx, they are synthesized on demand from membrane lipids, diffuse retrogradely across the synaptic cleft, and bind to presynaptic CB1 receptors to inhibit further neurotransmitter exocytosis (depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition or excitation / DSI/DSE).

stem: A 3-year-old child with severe Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy) experiences multiple daily refractory seizures. The pediatric neurologist prescribes Epidiolex, an FDA-approved pharmaceutical formulation of a non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid. What is the active pharmaceutical agent in this medication?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cannabidiol (CBD).

Epidiolex is a plant-derived, highly purified oral formulation of Cannabidiol (CBD):
• Non-intoxicating: CBD has low affinity for CB1/CB2 receptors and does not cause intoxication or euphoria.
• Indications: FDA-approved for refractory seizures associated with Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
• Proposed mechanisms: Antagonism of GPR55 receptors, TRPV1 desensitization, and modulation of intracellular calcium.

stem: Synthetic cannabinoids (such as 'K2' or 'Spice') are chemically distinct from natural plant-derived phytocannabinoids. In contrast to natural THC, synthetic cannabinoids frequently produce life-threatening toxicities including extreme agitation, delirium, severe psychosis, acute renal failure, and seizures. What pharmacological property accounts for their markedly increased toxicity?

options.text: They act as partial antagonists at CB1 receptors with slow receptor binding
They are high-potency, full agonists at CB1 receptors with up to 100-fold higher affinity than THC
They selectively activate peripheral CB2 receptors without CNS penetration
They are irreversible inhibitors of monoamine oxidase
They act purely as competitive antagonists at dopamine D2 receptors

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. They are high-potency, full agonists at CB1 receptors with up to 100-fold higher affinity than THC.

Pharmacological differences between natural THC and synthetic cannabinoids:
• Natural THC is a low-efficacy PARTIAL agonist at the CB1 receptor.
• Synthetic cannabinoids (e.g., JWH-018, AB-PINACA) are FULL, high-affinity agonists at CB1 receptors (often 50-100 times more potent than THC). Furthermore, natural cannabis contains cannabidiol (CBD), which modulates and buffers the adverse effects of THC; synthetic blends lack CBD and contain unregulated, highly toxic full agonists that cause profound hyperpyrexia, seizures, psychosis, and death.

stem: Anandamide is degraded and cleared from the synaptic cleft primarily through enzymatic hydrolysis by which membrane-bound intracellular enzyme?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH).

Endocannabinoid degradation:
• Anandamide (AEA) is degraded primarily by Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase (FAAH) into arachidonic acid and ethanolamine.
• 2-Arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) is degraded primarily by Monoacylglycerol Lipase (MAGL) into arachidonic acid and glycerol.
Pharmacological inhibition of FAAH or MAGL increases endogenous cannabinoid tone and is an active area of investigation for non-opioid analgesia.

stem: Dronabinol is an FDA-approved oral medication identical to synthetic delta-9-THC. For which of the following clinical indications is dronabinol approved in modern medical practice?

options.text: Major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety
Chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and anorexia/cachexia associated with AIDS

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and anorexia/cachexia associated with AIDS.

Dronabinol (and nabilone) are oral cannabinoid agonists approved for:
1. Prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) in patients who have failed conventional antiemetics.
2. Anorexia associated with weight loss in patients with AIDS (appetite stimulation / orexigenic effect via hypothalamic CB1 stimulation).

stem: Which cannabinoid receptor antagonist was previously developed as an anti-obesity drug but was withdrawn from the market worldwide due to severe adverse psychiatric effects, including profound depression, severe anxiety, and increased risk of suicide?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Rimonabant.

Rimonabant is a selective CB1 receptor inverse agonist. By blocking CB1 receptors in the hypothalamus and mesolimbic reward system, it suppressed appetite and promoted weight loss. However, it also blocked endogenous endocannabinoid tone necessary for mood regulation and reward, causing severe depressive symptoms, severe anxiety, and suicidal ideation, leading to its global withdrawal.

stem: A 19-year-old man undergoes urine drug testing for employment. He last smoked cannabis 2 weeks ago and has not consumed any since. His urine immunoassay test returns strongly positive for cannabinoids. What pharmacokinetic property of THC accounts for its prolonged detection window in urine for weeks after the last use in chronic users?

options.text: Irreversible covalent binding to serum albumin
High lipophilicity with extensive sequestration in adipose tissue and slow terminal elimination
Absence of hepatic metabolism by cytochrome P450 enzymes
Active reabsorption across renal collecting duct aquaporin channels

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. High lipophilicity with extensive sequestration in adipose tissue and slow terminal elimination.

THC is extraordinarily lipophilic (octanol-water partition coefficient > 6000):
• After inhalation or ingestion, it rapidly distributes into highly vascular tissues, followed by extensive accumulation and storage in body fat (adipose tissue).
• In chronic users, THC slowly leaches back from adipose stores into the bloodstream over days to weeks.
• The primary inactive metabolite, 11-nor-9-carboxy-THC (THC-COOH), is conjugated with glucuronic acid and excreted in urine, remaining detectable for 30 days or longer in chronic heavy users.

stem: Which of the following brain regions exhibits the highest density of cannabinoid CB1 receptors, explaining why acute cannabis intoxication produces significant impairments in working memory, attention, and executive cognitive functioning?

options.text: Hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and basal ganglia
Ventral tegmental area dopaminergic cell bodies

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and basal ganglia.

CB1 receptor distribution in the brain:
• High density: Hippocampus (impairs short-term memory consolidation), prefrontal cortex (impairs executive decision-making and attention), basal ganglia and cerebellum (causes psychomotor slowing and impaired coordination).
• Strikingly LOW density: Brainstem cardiorespiratory centers (pons and medulla). This physiological absence of CB1 receptors in the respiratory control centers explains why fatal respiratory depression does not occur with cannabis overdose alone (unlike opioids or barbiturates).

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents to the ED with severe anxiety and panic attacks after using cannabis. She reports seeing shadows moving and hearing whispering voices. Her brother has schizophrenia. Epidemiological studies demonstrate that heavy adolescent cannabis use is associated with a significant increase in the risk of developing which psychiatric disorder in genetically susceptible individuals?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Schizophrenia (chronic psychotic disorder).

Extensive epidemiological and genetic evidence shows that heavy cannabis use during adolescence (a critical period of neurodevelopment and synaptic pruning) is a dose-dependent environmental risk factor for the earlier onset and development of Schizophrenia and chronic psychotic disorders in genetically predisposed individuals (e.g., carrying polymorphisms in the COMT or AKT1 genes).

stem: Delta-9-THC is primarily metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P450 enzymes. Which active metabolite is formed by hepatic CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 oxidation, penetrates the blood-brain barrier rapidly, and has equal or greater psychoactive potency than parent THC?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. 11-hydroxy-THC (11-OH-THC).

When cannabis is ingested orally (edibles), THC undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to form 11-hydroxy-THC (11-OH-THC). 11-OH-THC is highly potent, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, and contributes significantly to the delayed, intense, and prolonged psychoactive effects characteristic of oral edibles compared to inhalation.

stem: Which of the following physiological effects on the cardiovascular system is most consistently observed following acute cannabis smoking in healthy adults?

options.text: Tachycardia and peripheral vasodilation with potential orthostatic hypotension
Pronounced coronary vasodilation without changes in heart rate
Decreased cardiac output and reduced myocardial oxygen demand

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Tachycardia and peripheral vasodilation with potential orthostatic hypotension.

Acute cardiovascular effects of cannabis:
• Dose-dependent resting tachycardia (heart rate increases by 20-50 bpm within minutes, mediated by sympathetic stimulation and parasympathetic withdrawal).
• Peripheral vasodilation (causing conjunctival injection and facial flushing).
• Orthostatic hypotension upon standing (which can precipitate syncope in naive users).
• In patients with pre-existing coronary artery disease, increased myocardial oxygen demand can trigger acute myocardial infarction.

stem: A 25-year-old patient in the emergency department with severe, intractable cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome has failed ondansetron, metoclopramide, and promethazine. Which of the following topical therapies applied to the abdomen or back provides rapid symptomatic relief by acting on TRPV1 receptors?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Capsaicin 0.025%–0.075% cream.

Topical capsaicin cream is a highly effective, evidence-based rescue treatment for acute Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS) in the ED:
• Capsaicin binds to and activates Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) receptors in the skin, mimicking the sensation of heat provided by hot showers.
• TRPV1 activation normalizes hypothalamic thermoregulatory signaling and decreases substance P release, breaking the cycle of nausea and vomiting.

stem: In addition to delta-9-THC and CBD, the Cannabis sativa plant contains more than 100 other phytocannabinoids and aromatic terpenes. Which of the following terpenes is commonly found in cannabis, mangoes, and hops, and is believed to contribute to the sedative effects of certain cannabis strains?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Myrcene.

Myrcene (beta-myrcene) is the most abundant terpene found in Cannabis sativa (as well as mangoes, hops, and lemongrass). It produces a characteristic earthy, musky aroma and contributes to muscle relaxation, sedation ('couch-lock'), and enhanced blood-brain barrier permeability via the proposed 'entourage effect.'

stem: Cannabinoid receptor type 2 (CB2) is structurally homologous to CB1 but exhibits a completely different anatomical distribution. CB2 receptors are primarily localized to which of the following tissues?

options.text: Cells of the immune system (spleen, tonsils, B-cells, macrophages, and microglia)

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cells of the immune system (spleen, tonsils, B-cells, macrophages, and microglia).

CB2 receptors are predominantly peripheral cannabinoid receptors expressed at high levels in immune and hematopoietic cells (macrophages, B-cells, T-cells, spleen, tonsils) and activated CNS microglia. Unlike CB1 receptors, activation of CB2 receptors modulates cytokine release and immune responses without producing psychoactive effects or intoxication.

stem: Which of the following behavioral interventions has the strongest clinical evidence base for the treatment of Cannabis Use Disorder (CUD)?

options.text: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET), and Contingency Management (CM)

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET), and Contingency Management (CM).

There are currently no FDA-approved medications for the treatment of Cannabis Use Disorder. The gold standard evidence-based treatments are psychosocial and behavioral interventions:
• Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Teaches coping strategies, craving management, and relapse prevention.
• Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET): Resolves ambivalence regarding quitting.
• Contingency Management (CM): Provides tangible rewards for confirmed negative toxicology screens.

stem: What is the primary cellular signaling cascade initiated when delta-9-THC binds to the Gi/o-protein coupled CB1 receptor on a presynaptic nerve terminal?

options.text: Activation of adenylyl cyclase, increased cAMP, and opening of L-type calcium channels
Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, decreased cAMP, inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels, and activation of inwardly rectifying potassium channels
Activation of phospholipase C, generation of IP3 and DAG, and intracellular calcium surge
Direct opening of a non-selective cation channel pore conducting sodium and calcium

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, decreased cAMP, inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels, and activation of inwardly rectifying potassium channels.

CB1 receptor downstream signaling:
• Coupling: Pertussis toxin-sensitive inhibitory Gi/o protein.
• Alpha-subunit: Inhibits adenylyl cyclase, decreasing cyclic AMP (cAMP) and protein kinase A (PKA) activity.
• Beta-gamma subunit: Directly inhibits presynaptic voltage-gated N-type and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels (reducing exocytotic neurotransmitter release) and stimulates G-protein inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels, causing membrane hyperpolarization.

stem: A 17-year-old driver is involved in a motor vehicle collision. Blood testing confirms acute delta-9-THC intoxication. Which of the following psychomotor impairments is most directly responsible for the increased risk of vehicular crashes associated with acute cannabis consumption?

options.text: Impaired divided attention, delayed reaction time, and lane-weaving (decreased tracking ability)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Impaired divided attention, delayed reaction time, and lane-weaving (decreased tracking ability).

Acute cannabis-induced driving impairment:
• Psychomotor effects: Increased reaction time, impaired divided attention (inability to process multiple visual inputs simultaneously), impaired tracking/lane-keeping ability, and distorted perception of speed and time.
• Risk: Increases crash risk approximately 2-fold, and synergistically increases risk when combined with alcohol.

stem: A 28-year-old man is found unresponsive in an alley. Physical examination reveals a respiratory rate of 4 breaths/minute, pinpoint pupils (miosis, 1 mm bilaterally), cold clammy skin, and cyanosis. Intravenous naloxone is administered, and within 90 seconds, the patient awakens, his pupils dilate, and his respiratory rate increases to 16 breaths/minute. What is the mechanism of action of naloxone?

options.text: Competitive antagonist at mu-, kappa-, and delta-opioid receptors with highest affinity for mu
Direct stimulant of the medullary pre-Bötzinger respiratory complex

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Competitive antagonist at mu-, kappa-, and delta-opioid receptors with highest affinity for mu.

Naloxone is a pure, short-acting competitive opioid receptor antagonist with high affinity for mu-opioid receptors (and lower affinity for kappa and delta receptors). It rapidly displaces opioid agonists from the receptor, reversing life-threatening opioid overdose signs (respiratory depression, coma, miosis). Because naloxone has a short half-life (~30-90 minutes), patients who ingested long-acting opioids (e.g., methadone) must be monitored closely for recurrent respiratory arrest.

stem: Opioid receptors (mu, delta, kappa) are G-protein coupled receptors coupled to Gi/o proteins. When an opioid agonist binds to the mu-opioid receptor, which two downstream ion channel events occur in the presynaptic terminal and postsynaptic neuron, respectively, to inhibit pain transmission?

options.text: Presynaptic: Opening of calcium channels; Postsynaptic: Closure of potassium channels
Presynaptic: Closure of voltage-gated calcium channels; Postsynaptic: Opening of inwardly rectifying potassium channels
Presynaptic: Influx of sodium; Postsynaptic: Efflux of chloride
Presynaptic: Opening of chloride channels; Postsynaptic: Influx of calcium
Presynaptic: Inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase; Postsynaptic: Activation of NMDA receptors

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Presynaptic: Closure of voltage-gated calcium channels; Postsynaptic: Opening of inwardly rectifying potassium channels.

Cellular mechanism of opioid action:
• Presynaptic inhibition: Activation of Gi/o-coupled mu-opioid receptors closes voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in primary nociceptive terminals, preventing Ca2+ influx and blocking the exocytosis of excitatory neurotransmitters (substance P, glutamate, CGRP).
• Postsynaptic inhibition: In postsynaptic projection neurons, beta-gamma subunits directly open G-protein coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channels, allowing K+ efflux. This hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane, rendering it refractory to excitatory input.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has been taking escalating doses of oral morphine for 6 months. She has developed significant pharmacological tolerance to most of the analgesic and adverse effects of morphine. Which of the following physiological effects of opioids NEVER develops tolerance, regardless of treatment duration?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Miosis (pupillary constriction) and constipation.

Opioid tolerance development:
• High tolerance develops rapidly to: Analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, nausea, and vomiting.
• Minimal or NO tolerance develops to:
  1. Miosis (pinpoint pupils via Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic nucleus stimulation).
  2. Constipation (decreased peristalsis and secretomotor inhibition in enteric nervous system).
Therefore, all patients on chronic opioid therapy require prophylactic bowel regimens (e.g., senna, docusate, polyethylene glycol, or peripheral mu-antagonists like methylnaltrexone).

stem: Which of the following endogenous opioid peptides is derived from the prohormone pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), possesses the highest affinity for mu-opioid receptors, and is synthesized in the anterior pituitary alongside adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Beta-endorphin.

Endogenous opioid peptides and precursors:
• Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC): Cleaved to produce Beta-endorphin (potent mu-agonist), ACTH, and alpha-MSH in the pituitary and arcuate nucleus.
• Proenkephalin: Cleaved to produce Met-enkephalin and Leu-enkephalin (preferential delta-opioid receptor agonists).
• Prodynorphin: Cleaved to produce Dynorphin A and B (preferential kappa-opioid receptor agonists, which mediate dysphoria).

stem: A 35-year-old man with opioid use disorder who is dependent on intravenous heroin is given an injection of buprenorphine. Within 45 minutes, he develops severe gooseflesh (piloerection), pupillary dilation (mydriasis), diarrhea, lacrimation, severe abdominal cramping, and muscle aches. Why did buprenorphine precipitate acute opioid withdrawal in this patient?

options.text: Buprenorphine is an irreversible antagonist at all opioid receptors
Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist with high receptor affinity that displaces full agonists
Buprenorphine blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the nucleus accumbens
Buprenorphine accelerates renal clearance of heroin
Buprenorphine is metabolized into naloxone in vivo

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist with high receptor affinity that displaces full agonists.

Buprenorphine has two critical pharmacological properties:
1. Extremely high binding affinity for the mu-opioid receptor (higher than heroin, morphine, or methadone).
2. Low intrinsic activity (partial agonist).
When administered to a patient who has active full mu-opioid agonists on their receptors, buprenorphine avidly binds and displaces the full agonist. Because its intrinsic efficacy is lower, the net level of mu-opioid receptor activation abruptly drops, precipitating acute precipitated withdrawal. Therefore, buprenorphine must only be initiated when the patient is already in mild-to-moderate spontaneous withdrawal (COWS score ≥ 8-12).

stem: Suboxone is a combination medication used for the maintenance treatment of opioid use disorder. It contains buprenorphine and naloxone in a 4:1 ratio. What is the clinical rationale for including naloxone in this sublingual formulation?

options.text: To increase the oral absorption of buprenorphine
To prevent intravenous abuse; naloxone has poor sublingual bioavailability but precipitates withdrawal if injected
To prevent buprenorphine from crossing the blood-brain barrier

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. To prevent intravenous abuse; naloxone has poor sublingual bioavailability but precipitates withdrawal if injected.

Pharmacological design of Suboxone (buprenorphine/naloxone):
• When taken sublingually as prescribed: Buprenorphine is absorbed across the oral mucosa, while naloxone has near-zero sublingual bioavailability (<5%) and undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, producing therapeutic buprenorphine maintenance without interference.
• If crushed and injected intravenously: Naloxone becomes 100% bioavailable, immediately blocking opioid receptors and precipitating severe, unpleasant withdrawal, thereby strongly deterring intravenous diversion and abuse.

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic severe pain is prescribed methadone. In addition to serving as a potent, long-acting full mu-opioid receptor agonist, methadone possesses which additional unique pharmacological property that makes it effective for neuropathic pain but warrants routine baseline electrocardiograms?

options.text: NMDA receptor antagonist and serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; hERG channel block causing QT prolongation
Dopamine reuptake inhibitor; Delta wave on ECG
Muscarinic M2 receptor agonist; Ventricular pre-excitation

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. NMDA receptor antagonist and serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; hERG channel block causing QT prolongation.

Methadone unique pharmacology:
• Full mu-opioid agonist with long elimination half-life (24-60 hours).
• Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist: Prevents central sensitization and opioid tolerance, making it uniquely effective in refractory neuropathic pain.
• Inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake.
• Cardiotoxicity: Blocks cardiac hERG potassium channels, causing QT interval prolongation and torsades de pointes (ventricular tachycardia). Baseline and follow-up ECG monitoring is recommended.

stem: Which of the following synthetic opioids is 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine, is highly lipophilic with a rapid onset (within 1–2 minutes), and can cause fatal wooden chest syndrome (thoracoabdominal muscle rigidity preventing mechanical ventilation) when administered rapidly as an intravenous bolus?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Fentanyl.

Fentanyl is a synthetic phenylpiperidine opioid:
• Potency: ~100 times more potent than morphine due to high lipophilicity.
• Rapid bolus adverse effect: 'Wooden chest syndrome' (severe chest wall and abdominal muscle rigidity mediated by central striatal and locus coeruleus pathways), which impairs chest expansion and prevents bag-valve-mask ventilation. Treatment is immediate administration of naloxone and/or a neuromuscular blocker.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease receives multiple doses of meperidine (pethidine) for post-surgical pain. Two days later, she develops severe myoclonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Accumulation of which neurotoxic metabolite caused her seizures?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Normeperidine.

Meperidine is metabolized in the liver via N-demethylation to Normeperidine, an active metabolite with a long half-life (15-30 hours). Normeperidine has minimal analgesic effect but is a potent central nervous system convulsant. In renal impairment or with repeated dosing, normeperidine accumulates, causing tremors, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, and grand mal seizures. Naloxone does not reverse (and may worsen) normeperidine-induced seizures.

stem: Which of the following peripheral mu-opioid receptor antagonists is quaternary and permanently charged, preventing it from crossing the blood-brain barrier, allowing it to treat opioid-induced constipation without reversing central analgesia or precipitating opioid withdrawal?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Methylnaltrexone.

Methylnaltrexone (and naloxegol) is a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA). The addition of a methyl group to the amine ring confers a permanent positive charge, preventing the molecule from crossing the blood-brain barrier. It selectively blocks gastrointestinal mu-opioid receptors, restoring bowel motility in opioid-induced constipation without reversing central analgesia or causing withdrawal.

stem: Morphine undergoes phase II hepatic glucuronidation to produce two major metabolites: morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G). Which statement regarding M6G is pharmacologically correct?

options.text: M6G is an inactive metabolite with no biological activity
M6G is a potent analgesic that accumulates in renal failure to cause prolonged sedation and respiratory depression
M6G is a pure antagonist that precipitates acute withdrawal
M6G is primarily excreted in expired air via the lungs
M6G produces neuroexcitation and hyperalgesia without analgesia

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. M6G is a potent analgesic that accumulates in renal failure to cause prolonged sedation and respiratory depression.

Morphine metabolism:
• Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G, ~10%): Active metabolite with high mu-opioid affinity and potent analgesic efficacy (more potent than morphine itself). It is cleared by the kidneys; in renal insufficiency, M6G accumulates, causing prolonged sedation and life-threatening respiratory depression.
• Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G, ~60%): Lacks opioid analgesic activity and causes neuroexcitation, allodynia, and myoclonus.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with acute abdominal pain and diarrhea. He takes loperamide. Loperamide is an effective antidiarrheal agent that acts as a mu-opioid agonist in the myenteric plexus. Why does loperamide not produce central euphoria or analgesia at therapeutic doses?

options.text: It is an antagonist at central mu-opioid receptors
It is actively extruded from the brain across the blood-brain barrier by P-glycoprotein efflux pumps
It is completely destroyed by gastric acid
It binds exclusively to kappa-opioid receptors

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. It is actively extruded from the brain across the blood-brain barrier by P-glycoprotein efflux pumps.

Loperamide is a potent mu-opioid receptor agonist in the gastrointestinal myenteric plexus (slowing peristalsis and extending transit time). Although lipophilic, any drug that crosses into brain capillary endothelial cells is actively and efficiently pumped back into the blood by the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Consequently, brain levels remain negligible at standard therapeutic doses, preventing euphoria and addiction. (Massive supratherapeutic doses saturate P-glycoprotein, causing CNS opioid effects and fatal QTc prolongation/cardiac arrest).

stem: Which of the following prodrug opioids must be metabolized in the liver by Cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) into morphine to achieve its primary analgesic effect, explaining why CYP2D6 'ultra-rapid metabolizers' are at high risk of fatal respiratory depression?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Codeine.

Codeine (3-methylmorphine) is a weak prodrug with low intrinsic affinity for mu-receptors (~200-fold less than morphine). It requires O-demethylation to active Morphine by CYP2D6:
• Poor metabolizers (~7-10% of Caucasians): Lack functional CYP2D6 and experience little to no pain relief.
• Ultra-rapid metabolizers (gene duplication, up to 30% in North African/Middle Eastern populations): Rapidly convert codeine into high, toxic concentrations of morphine. Nursing mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers pass lethal concentrations of morphine in breast milk to their infants.

stem: Tramadol provides analgesia through a dual mechanism: weak agonism at mu-opioid receptors and inhibition of the reuptake of which two neurotransmitters?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Serotonin and norepinephrine.

Tramadol is an atypical centrally acting analgesic with a dual mechanism:
1. Its active metabolite (O-desmethyltramadol / M1, formed via CYP2D6) is a mu-opioid receptor agonist.
2. The parent drug inhibits the neuronal reuptake of both Serotonin (5-HT) and Norepinephrine (NE), potentiating descending spinal pain-inhibitory pathways.
• Risks: Lowers the seizure threshold and can precipitate Serotonin Syndrome when combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, or triptans.

stem: Which opioid receptor subtype, when selectively stimulated by dynorphins or synthetic agonists such as pentazocine and salvinorin A, produces spinal analgesia accompanied by dysphoria, hallucinations, and depersonalization rather than euphoria?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Kappa-opioid receptor (KOR).

• Mu receptors (MOR): Mediate supraspinal analgesia, euphoria, physical dependence, miosis, constipation, and respiratory depression.
• Kappa receptors (KOR): Mediate spinal analgesia, miosis, sedation, and characteristically DYSPHORIA, psychotomimetic hallucinations, and anxiety (by inhibiting dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens). Dynorphins are the endogenous ligands.
• Delta receptors (DOR): Mediate analgesia and modulate emotional responses.

stem: Following intravenous administration of morphine, a patient develops localized pruritus, flushing, warm skin, and mild bronchospasm. Blood pressure drops slightly. This reaction is non-immunologic (not IgE-mediated) and occurs through which mechanism?

options.text: Direct activation of H1 receptors by morphine
Direct non-allergic mast cell degranulation via MRGPRX2 receptors with histamine release

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Direct non-allergic mast cell degranulation via MRGPRX2 receptors with histamine release.

Natural and semi-synthetic phenanthrene opioids (morphine, codeine, meperidine) can directly stimulate cutaneous mast cells via Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2), triggering non-IgE-mediated histamine release. This pseudo-allergic reaction causes pruritus, urticaria, facial flushing, hypotension, and mild bronchospasm. In contrast, synthetic opioids (such as fentanyl) do not trigger histamine release.

stem: Naltrexone is an orally bioavailable, long-acting opioid receptor antagonist with a half-life of approximately 10 hours. In addition to preventing relapse in detoxified opioid-dependent individuals, naltrexone is FDA-approved for the treatment of which other substance use disorder?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Alcohol use disorder.

Naltrexone is FDA-approved for Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD):
• Mechanism: Alcohol consumption stimulates endogenous beta-endorphin release, which disinhibits dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) to produce reinforcing euphoria. Naltrexone blocks mu-opioid receptors, eliminating the positive reinforcing reward and euphoria of alcohol, thereby reducing cravings and heavy drinking days.

stem: In the brainstem, which neural region is responsible for the blunting of hypercapnic and hypoxic ventilatory drive during opioid-induced respiratory depression?

options.text: Pre-Bötzinger complex and medullary respiratory rhythm generator
Pneumotaxic center in the rostral pons

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Pre-Bötzinger complex and medullary respiratory rhythm generator.

Opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD) is the leading cause of death in opioid overdose:
• Mu-opioid receptors are densely expressed in the Pre-Bötzinger complex (the pacemaker for inspiratory rhythm) and ventral respiratory group in the medulla.
• Agonist binding hyperpolarizes rhythm-generating neurons, decreasing respiratory frequency and blunting the medullary chemoreceptor response to rising PaCO2.

stem: A 40-year-old patient who had been taking high-dose oxycodone for 6 months stops abruptly. Within 24 hours, he develops severe autonomic hyperarousal, diaphoresis, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, piloerection ('cold turkey'), tachycardia, and hypertension. This physical withdrawal syndrome is driven primarily by rebound hyperactivity of which central noradrenergic nucleus?

options.text: Locus coeruleus in the rostral pons

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Locus coeruleus in the rostral pons.

Pathophysiology of opioid withdrawal:
• Chronic opioid exposure chronically inhibits the noradrenergic Locus Coeruleus (LC). In response, LC neurons homeostatically upregulate adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A.
• When the opioid is abruptly withdrawn, this chronic inhibition is lifted, causing massive rebound noradrenergic hyperactivity from the locus coeruleus.
• Alpha-2 adrenergic agonists (Clonidine or Lofexidine) bind to inhibitory presynaptic alpha-2 receptors on LC neurons, suppressing this sympathetic outflow and relieving withdrawal symptoms.

stem: Which of the following mixed opioid agonist-antagonists acts as a kappa-opioid receptor agonist and a weak mu-opioid receptor partial agonist/antagonist, and is used for moderate pain or labor analgesia with a lower ceiling for respiratory depression?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Butorphanol (or Nalbuphine).

Butorphanol and Nalbuphine are mixed opioid agonist-antagonists:
• Kappa agonist: Produces analgesia.
• Mu partial agonist or antagonist: Exhibits a 'ceiling effect' for respiratory depression (less lethal overdose risk), but can precipitate acute withdrawal if administered to patients physically dependent on full mu-opioid agonists.

stem: A 22-year-old man involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision is brought to the trauma bay. On examination, he opens his eyes only in response to painful sternal rub, utters inappropriate disorganized words, and flexes his elbows and wrists abnormally (decorticate posturing) in response to pain. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. GCS 8 (Severe TBI).

Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) calculation (E + V + M):
• Eye opening (E, max 4): Opens eyes to pain = 2 points.
• Verbal response (V, max 5): Inappropriate words = 3 points.
• Motor response (M, max 6): Abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) = 3 points.
Total Score = 2 + 3 + 3 = 8.
• A GCS of ≤ 8 defines Severe Traumatic Brain Injury and represents an indication for definitive endotracheal intubation ('GCS of 8, intubate').

stem: An unconscious patient with severe traumatic brain injury displays abnormal decerebrate (extensor) posturing (arms adducted and internally rotated, elbows rigidly extended, wrists pronated and flexed). Decerebrate posturing indicates a compressive lesion or herniation disrupting the brainstem at which level?

options.text: Brainstem below the red nucleus (upper pons or lower midbrain)

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Brainstem below the red nucleus (upper pons or lower midbrain).

Posturing in brain herniation and coma:
• Decorticate posturing (flexor posturing): Lesions ABOVE the red nucleus (cerebral cortex or internal capsule). Rubrospinal tract is intact, maintaining flexor tone in upper extremities.
• Decerebrate posturing (extensor posturing): Lesions AT OR BELOW the red nucleus (midbrain-pons junction). Rubrospinal facilitatory flexor drive is lost, leaving unopposed vestibulospinal and reticulospinal drive that causes rigid extension of all extremities. Decerebrate carries a worse prognosis.

stem: A 30-year-old construction worker falls from a scaffolding and strikes his head. In the emergency department, his blood pressure increases from 125/80 to 195/105 mm Hg, his heart rate drops from 82 to 44 bpm, and his breathing pattern becomes irregular with periods of apnea (Cheyne-Stokes respirations). What physiological phenomenon is this patient exhibiting, and what does it indicate?

options.text: Bezold-Jarisch reflex; Acute inferior wall myocardial infarction
Cushing triad; Severe intracranial hypertension with impending brain herniation
Brown-Séquard syndrome; High cervical cord transection
Spinal shock; Loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cushing triad; Severe intracranial hypertension with impending brain herniation.

Cushing Triad is a late, ominous physiological response to severely elevated intracranial pressure (ICP):
1. Hypertension with widened pulse pressure (cerebral ischemia triggers massive sympathetic outflow to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure [CPP = MAP - ICP]).
2. Bradycardia (carotid baroreceptors sense severe systemic hypertension and trigger vagal parasympathetic reflex slowing of heart rate).
3. Irregular respirations (brainstem compression disrupts respiratory rhythm generators in the medulla).
It signals imminent life-threatening cerebral herniation.

stem: In uncal (transtentorial) herniation, the medial temporal lobe (uncus) herniates downward over the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli. Which cranial nerve is compressed earliest by the herniating uncus, and what is the characteristic clinical finding?

options.text: Abducens nerve (CN VI); Inability to abduct the contralateral eye
Oculomotor nerve (CN III); Ipsilateral pupillary dilation and unresponsiveness to light ('blown pupil')
Trochlear nerve (CN IV); Diplopia on downgaze
Facial nerve (CN VII); Ipsilateral complete facial paralysis
Trigeminal nerve (CN V); Loss of sensation on the cheek

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Oculomotor nerve (CN III); Ipsilateral pupillary dilation and unresponsiveness to light ('blown pupil').

Uncal (transtentorial) herniation sequence:
1. The herniating medial temporal uncus compresses the ipsilateral CN III against the tentorial edge. Because parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibers travel superficially on the outside of CN III, they are compressed first, causing ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil ('blown pupil').
2. Progressive compression knocks out somatic motor fibers of CN III ('down-and-out' eye).
3. Compression of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
4. Midbrain compression causes coma and secondary Duret flame-shaped hemorrhages.

stem: In severe uncal herniation, downward displacement of the midbrain can push the CONTRALATERAL cerebral peduncle against the opposite tentorial edge, causing ipsilateral hemiparesis (a false localizing motor sign). What is the anatomical term for this indentation in the contralateral cerebral peduncle?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Kernohan notch (Kernohan phenomenon).

Normally, a supratentorial mass on the left produces right-sided hemiparesis. However, in Kernohan phenomenon:
• Massive left uncal herniation shifts the midbrain laterally across the incisura, crushing the CONTRALATERAL (right) cerebral peduncle against the rigid right tentorial notch (creating 'Kernohan notch').
• Because the corticospinal fibers in the right peduncle cross downstream in the medulla to supply the left side of the body, the patient presents with hemiparesis IPSILATERAL to the mass (left-sided hemiparesis). This is a classic 'false-localizing' sign.

stem: A 19-year-old hockey player sustains a forceful check into the boards. He does not lose consciousness, but reports immediate headache, dizziness, disorientation, and retrograde amnesia for the game. Standard non-contrast head CT is completely normal. What is the fundamental cellular pathophysiology of concussion (mild traumatic brain injury)?

options.text: Macroscopic parenchymal shearing and intraparenchymal hematoma formation
Functional neurometabolic cascade characterized by ionic flux, indiscriminate glutamate release, and a cellular energy crisis
Primary demyelination of the corpus callosum
Rupture of the middle meningeal artery

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Functional neurometabolic cascade characterized by ionic flux, indiscriminate glutamate release, and a cellular energy crisis.

Concussion (mild TBI) is a functional neuronal disturbance rather than a structural lesion (explaining normal routine CT/MRI):
• Biomechanical shearing stretches axonal membranes, causing unregulated opening of ion channels and massive indiscriminate glutamate release.
• Widespread ionic flux occurs: efflux of K+ and influx of Ca2+.
• In an attempt to restore ionic equilibrium, Na+/K+ ATPase pumps work at maximum capacity, accelerating glycolysis (hyperglycolysis).
• This coincides with impaired cerebral blood flow, resulting in an acute cellular 'energy crisis' (ATP depletion and lactate accumulation).

stem: A 16-year-old football player sustains a concussion during a game on Friday. Against medical advice, he returns to play the following Tuesday while still experiencing mild headaches and dizziness. During the second game, he suffers a relatively minor tackle to the head. Within 2 minutes, he collapses, loses consciousness, displays rapidly expanding bilateral pupillary dilation, and develops respiratory arrest due to massive brain herniation. What catastrophic syndrome occurred?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Second impact syndrome.

Second Impact Syndrome occurs when a second head impact is sustained before the brain has fully recovered from a prior concussion (while the brain is still in a vulnerable metabolic state):
• Pathophysiology: Loss of cerebral autoregulation leads to massive, uncontrollable cerebral vascular engorgement, malignant intracranial hypertension, and fatal brain herniation within minutes.
• Mortality exceeds 50%, emphasizing the strict rule that no athlete should return to play while symptomatic from a concussion.

stem: An autopsy performed on a 48-year-old former professional NFL player who suffered from severe depression, memory loss, emotional instability, and dementia reveals prominent cerebral cortical atrophy, cavum septum pellucidum, and extensive perivascular neurofibrillary tangles. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates patchy deposition of hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons and astrocytes concentrated at the depths of cortical sulci. What is the neuropathological diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) is a progressive neurodegenerative tauopathy triggered by repetitive head impacts (subconcussive blows or concussions in boxers, football players, combat veterans):
• Diagnostic pathognomonic feature: Perivascular accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau (p-tau) neurofibrillary tangles in neurons and astrocytes located preferentially at the depths of cerebral sulci (unlike Alzheimer disease, which begins in the entorhinal cortex/hippocampus and features diffuse beta-amyloid plaques).

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with head trauma following an assault. Examination reveals ecchymosis over the mastoid process behind the ear (Battle sign), bilateral periorbital ecchymoses without local eye trauma ('raccoon eyes'), hemotympanum on otoscopy, and clear fluid dripping from his nose. What type of skull fracture has occurred?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Basilar skull fracture.

Basilar skull fracture (fracture involving the floor of the anterior, middle, or posterior cranial fossa):
• Classic clinical signs:
  1. Battle sign: Ecchymosis over the mastoid process (indicates temporal/petrous bone fracture).
  2. Raccoon eyes: Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (indicates anterior cranial fossa fracture).
  3. CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea (tearing of the adherent dura mater and arachnoid).
  4. Hemotympanum: Blood behind the tympanic membrane.
• Nasogastric tubes are strictly contraindicated (can enter the intracranial cavity through a fractured cribriform plate).

stem: A patient with suspected basilar skull fracture has persistent clear drainage from the right nostril. To definitively differentiate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from normal nasal mucus, laboratory analysis of the fluid should test for the presence of which highly specific biomarker?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Beta-2 transferrin (asialotransferrin).

Beta-2 transferrin (tau transferrin) is a desialylated isoform of transferrin produced exclusively within the central nervous system through neuraminidase activity in the brain. It is found uniquely in cerebrospinal fluid, perilymph, and aqueous humor, and is completely ABSENT from tears, nasal mucus, saliva, or blood. Testing for beta-2 transferrin via immunofixation electrophoresis is the gold standard for diagnosing CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea.

stem: In subfalcine (cingulate) herniation, a unilateral hemispheric mass displaces the cingulate gyrus beneath the rigid free lower edge of the falx cerebri. Compression of which cerebral artery during subfalcine herniation leads to ischemic infarction of the leg representation in the primary motor and sensory cortex?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation occurs when a unilateral mass shifts the cingulate gyrus across the midline under the rigid falx cerebri. As the tissue shifts, it compresses the ipsilateral (or both) Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) against the falx, resulting in frontal lobe ischemia and infarction of the paracentral lobule, clinically manifesting as contralateral lower extremity weakness and abulia.

stem: Which brain herniation syndrome involves downward herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, resulting in direct compression of the medulla oblongata, respiratory arrest, cardiac collapse, and rapid death?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Tonsillar herniation.

Tonsillar herniation involves the downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical spinal canal. This directly compresses the vital cardiorespiratory centers in the medulla oblongata, leading to abrupt apnea, bradycardia, hemodynamic collapse, and immediate death.

stem: In patients with acute severe traumatic brain injury and intracranial hypertension, Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) must be maintained above 60 mm Hg. What is the mathematical definition of Cerebral Perfusion Pressure?

options.text: CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) − Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
CPP = Diastolic Blood Pressure − Central Venous Pressure

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) − Intracranial Pressure (ICP).

Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) is the net pressure gradient driving cerebral blood flow to the brain:
CPP = MAP - ICP (or CVP, whichever is higher).
• Under normal conditions, ICP is ≤ 15 mm Hg and CPP is 70-90 mm Hg.
• In severe TBI, if ICP rises to 35 mm Hg and MAP is 85 mm Hg, CPP falls to 50 mm Hg (below the critical threshold of 60 mm Hg), causing secondary ischemic brain injury. Guidelines recommend maintaining CPP between 60 and 70 mm Hg.

stem: An intubated patient with severe traumatic brain injury develops an acute spike in intracranial pressure to 35 mm Hg. The physician temporarily hyperventilates the patient to an end-tidal PaCO2 of 30 mm Hg. By what physiological mechanism does acute hypercapnia versus hypocapnia alter intracranial pressure?

options.text: Hypocapnia causes cerebral arteriolar vasodilation; hypercapnia causes vasoconstriction
Hypocapnia causes cerebral arteriolar vasoconstriction (decreasing cerebral blood volume); hypercapnia causes vasodilation
Hypocapnia increases CSF secretion by the choroid plexus
Carbon dioxide has no effect on cerebral microvasculature
Hypocapnia causes systemic venous pooling in the extremities

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Hypocapnia causes cerebral arteriolar vasoconstriction (decreasing cerebral blood volume); hypercapnia causes vasodilation.

Cerebral blood flow (CBF) is exquisitely sensitive to arterial PaCO2:
• Rising PaCO2 (hypercapnia) drops perivascular pH, causing profound cerebral arteriolar vasodilation, increasing cerebral blood volume and dramatically raising ICP.
• Lowering PaCO2 (hypocapnia via hyperventilation, PaCO2 30-35 mm Hg) induces rapid cerebral arteriolar vasoconstriction, reducing intracranial blood volume and rapidly lowering ICP. (Excessive hyperventilation to PaCO2 < 30 mm Hg is avoided because severe vasoconstriction causes secondary brain ischemia).

stem: Which osmotic agent is an inert polysaccharide hexitol that is administered intravenously to treat acute cerebral edema by creating an intravascular osmotic gradient that draws free water from the brain parenchyma into the vascular compartment across an intact blood-brain barrier?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Mannitol.

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic (administered as 20% solution at 0.5-1.0 g/kg) used to reduce elevated ICP:
• Mechanism: Mannitol does not cross the intact blood-brain barrier. It creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out of swollen parenchymal brain cells into the intravascular space, shrinking brain volume.
• Secondary rheological effect: Decreases blood viscosity, promoting microvascular cerebral perfusion.
• Monitor: Serum osmolality (hold if >320 mOsm/kg) and renal function.

stem: In addition to mannitol, hypertonic saline (3% or 23.4% NaCl) is widely used for acute intracranial pressure crises. What is the major advantage of hypertonic saline over mannitol in a hypotensive trauma patient?

options.text: Hypertonic saline induces profound diuresis to lower blood pressure
Hypertonic saline expands intravascular volume and supports blood pressure without causing osmotic diuresis
Hypertonic saline easily crosses the blood-brain barrier
Hypertonic saline is metabolized in the liver into glucose
Hypertonic saline directly inhibits NMDA receptors

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Hypertonic saline expands intravascular volume and supports blood pressure without causing osmotic diuresis.

Hypertonic Saline (HTS) vs Mannitol in TBI:
• While mannitol causes significant osmotic diuresis that can precipitate hypovolemia and hypotension (which reduces cerebral perfusion pressure), hypertonic saline draws water into the intravascular space to expand circulating plasma volume, supporting mean arterial pressure (MAP) while simultaneously reducing cerebral edema and lowering ICP. It is especially preferred in multitrauma patients with hypovolemic shock.

stem: During rapid deceleration in a motor vehicle collision, the moving head strikes the steering wheel. The brain sustains a contusion at the site of impact, as well as a second contusion directly opposite the impact site as the brain rebounds within the skull. What are the terms for the impact injury and the opposite rebound injury, respectively?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Coup injury and Contrecoup injury.

Cerebral contusions (bruising of the brain surface):
• Coup injury: Occurs directly beneath the point of skull impact as the inward-bending calvarium compresses the underlying cortical crests.
• Contrecoup injury: Occurs on the brain surface directly opposite the site of impact as the brain decelerates and rebounds violently against the opposing bony inner surface of the skull (often against the irregular sphenoid wings or cribriform plate).

stem: Following severe closed head trauma, secondary brain injury develops over hours to days. Which of the following systemic secondary insults is the most potent contributor to secondary neuronal death and must be rigorously prevented in neurotrauma resuscitation?

options.text: Hypotension (Systolic BP < 90 mm Hg) and Hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mm Hg)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Hypotension (Systolic BP < 90 mm Hg) and Hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mm Hg).

Primary TBI occurs at the moment of impact and cannot be reversed. Resuscitation focuses entirely on preventing secondary brain injury:
• A single episode of hypotension (SBP < 90 mm Hg) in severe TBI doubles mortality.
• Hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mm Hg or SpO2 < 90%) significantly worsens neurological outcomes.
• When combined, hypotension and hypoxemia result in a greater than 75% mortality rate, making airway stabilization and hemodynamic volume resuscitation the highest clinical priorities.

stem: Which of the following monitoring devices is considered the gold standard for continuous intracranial pressure (ICP) measurement because it allows both accurate pressure monitoring and therapeutic drainage of cerebrospinal fluid?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Intraventricular catheter / External ventricular drain (EVD).

An external ventricular drain (EVD / ventriculostomy) is the gold standard for ICP monitoring because it is inserted directly into the lateral ventricle, providing highly accurate global intracranial pressure readings while uniquely offering therapeutic capability: draining CSF to immediately reduce elevated ICP.

stem: Secondary flame-shaped, linear hemorrhages occurring in the midline of the midbrain and upper pons in patients with rapidly progressing descending central or uncal transtentorial herniation are known eponymously as:
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Duret hemorrhages.

Duret hemorrhages are secondary brainstem hemorrhages (linear or flame-shaped) located in the paramedian midbrain and upper pons. As descending transtentorial herniation shifts the brainstem caudally, the basilar artery (fixed to the skull base) remains tethered, stretching and tearing small penetrating paramedian branches of the basilar artery, leading to fatal brainstem necrosis.

stem: A 22-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of high fever, severe headache, confusion, and vomiting. Physical examination shows temperature 39.4°C, heart rate 124 bpm, blood pressure 85/55 mm Hg, marked nuchal rigidity, and petechial purpuric skin lesions on his trunk and lower extremities. What is the most likely causative organism, and what is its Gram-stain morphology?

options.text: Neisseria meningitidis; Gram-negative kidney bean-shaped diplococci

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Neisseria meningitidis; Gram-negative kidney bean-shaped diplococci.

Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus):
• Demographics: Common cause of epidemic bacterial meningitis in young adults living in crowded quarters (dorms, military barracks).
• Hallmark: Petechial or purpuric rash (due to meningococcemia and lipooligosaccharide / LOS endotoxin-mediated endothelial injury and DIC).
• Morphology: Gram-negative, kidney-bean-shaped diplococci found intracellularly within neutrophils.
• Complication: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, acute adrenal failure, and circulatory collapse).

stem: A 6-day-old neonate presents with lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia (35.6°C), and a bulging anterior fontanelle. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grows Gram-positive, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-resistant cocci in chains that produce a positive CAMP test (augmented hemolysis with Staphylococcus aureus). Which organism is the most common cause of neonatal bacterial meningitis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus / GBS).

Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep / GBS) is the #1 cause of neonatal meningitis and sepsis (<1 month of age), followed by Escherichia coli (K1 capsular antigen) and Listeria monocytogenes:
• Microbiological characteristics: Gram-positive cocci in chains, narrow zone of beta-hemolysis, bacitracin resistant, and CAMP test positive (CAMP factor enlarges the area of hemolysis formed by S. aureus beta-hemolysin into an arrow-head shape).
• Prevention: Universal maternal screening at 36-37 weeks with intrapartum IV penicillin/ampicillin prophylaxis.

stem: A 68-year-old renal transplant recipient on immunosuppressive therapy presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Gram stain of the CSF reveals Gram-positive rods with tumbling motility at room temperature (22°C) and cold enrichment growth. Which empiric antimicrobial agent MUST be added to the standard vancomycin and ceftriaxone regimen to cover this pathogen in patients >50 years or immunocompromised?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Ampicillin.

This patient has Listeria monocytogenes meningitis:
• Demographics: Neonates, adults >50 years, and immunocompromised patients.
• Microbiology: Facultative intracellular Gram-positive rod; exhibits 'tumbling motility' on wet mount at 22-25°C and can grow at refrigerator temperatures ('cold enrichment').
• Crucial therapeutic pearl: Listeria is intrinsically RESISTANT to all cephalosporins (including 3rd-generation cephalosporins like ceftriaxone) due to low affinity for penicillin-binding proteins. Therefore, AMPICILLIN must be added to empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone in patients >50 years, neonates, or immunocompromised individuals.

stem:
Lumbar puncture analysis in a 45-year-old man with fever and nuchal rigidity yields the following CSF results:
• Opening pressure: 310 mm H2O (normal 70–180)
• Leukocytes: 4,500/mm³ with 92% neutrophils
• Glucose: 18 mg/dL (serum glucose 110 mg/dL; ratio 0.16)
• Protein: 320 mg/dL (normal 15–45)
Which type of meningitis is unequivocally diagnosed by this CSF profile?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Acute bacterial meningitis.

CSF Profiles in Meningitis:
• Acute Bacterial: Opening pressure markedly ELEVATED (>200-300 mm H2O); WBC markedly ELEVATED (>1,000-10,000/μL) with Neutrophil predominance (>80%); Protein markedly ELEVATED (>100-500 mg/dL); Glucose markedly DECREASED (<40 mg/dL or CSF:serum ratio < 0.4).
• Viral (Aseptic): Normal or mildly elevated opening pressure; WBC 10-500/μL with Lymphocyte predominance; Protein mildly elevated (50-100 mg/dL); Glucose NORMAL (>60% of serum).
• Fungal/TB: Elevated opening pressure; WBC 100-500/μL (lymphocytic); Protein markedly elevated; Glucose DECREASED.

stem: An adult with suspected acute bacterial meningitis requires empiric antibiotic therapy. Randomized trials have demonstrated that administering intravenous dexamethasone either before or with the first dose of antibiotics significantly reduces hearing loss and neurological sequelae, particularly when the infection is caused by which pathogen?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Streptococcus pneumoniae.

In acute bacterial meningitis, antibiotic-induced bacterial lysis releases cell wall fragments (peptidoglycan and teichoic acid), triggering a massive inflammatory cytokine cascade (TNF-alpha and IL-1beta) in the subarachnoid space that worsens cerebral edema and sensorineural hearing loss. Administration of IV Dexamethasone (10 mg) before or simultaneously with the first dose of antibiotics blunts this inflammatory cascade, significantly reducing mortality and sensorineural hearing loss in adults with Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis.

stem: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 42 cells/mm³) presents with insidious headache, mild fever, and malaise. Lumbar puncture reveals elevated opening pressure (280 mm H2O). India ink staining of the CSF reveals round budding yeast cells surrounded by a wide, clear halo. What is the organism, and what is its capsule composed of?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cryptococcus neoformans; Glucuronoxylomannan polysaccharide capsule.

Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated opportunistic environmental yeast found in pigeon droppings):
• Clinical presentation: Subacute meningoencephalitis in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 < 100/μL).
• Microbiology: Thick antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule composed of Glucuronoxylomannan (GXM). 
• Diagnostics: India ink staining repels the capsule, producing a clear halo around the yeast; Cryptococcal Antigen (CrAg) latex agglutination or lateral flow assay has >95% sensitivity.
• Treatment: Induction with Amphotericin B + Flucytosine, followed by maintenance Fluconazole.

stem: Which physical examination sign is positive when passive flexion of the patient's neck causes involuntary, reflexive flexion of the hips and knees due to meningeal irritation?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Brudzinski sign.

Signs of meningeal irritation:
• Brudzinski sign: Involuntary flexion of the hips and knees when the examiner passively flexes the patient's neck in the supine position.
• Kernig sign: Resistance or pain in the hamstrings/lumbar spine upon passive extension of the knee when the patient's hip is flexed at 90 degrees.

stem: A 20-year-old college student is diagnosed with acute meningococcal meningitis. Public health authorities are notified to identify close contacts (roommates, dorm-mates, intimate contacts). Which of the following antimicrobial regimens is recommended as first-line chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of patients with Neisseria meningitidis infection?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Rifampin (or single-dose Ciprofloxacin or Ceftriaxone).

Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of Neisseria meningitidis:
• Indication: Household members, roommates, daycare contacts, or anyone directly exposed to oral secretions (intubation, resuscitation) within 7 days prior to onset.
• Regimens:
  1. Rifampin: 600 mg PO BID for 2 days (warn patient of orange discoloration of tears/urine).
