  2. Ciprofloxacin: Single 500 mg PO dose (in adults).
  3. Ceftriaxone: Single 250 mg IM dose (preferred in pregnancy).

stem: What is the most common viral etiology of acute aseptic meningitis in children and adults, accounting for over 85% of cases with identifiable viral causes, typically occurring in late summer and autumn?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Enteroviruses (Coxsackievirus, Echovirus, Poliovirus).

Enteroviruses (positive-sense, single-stranded, non-enveloped RNA picornaviruses—primarily Coxsackievirus B and Echoviruses) are responsible for >85-90% of all cases of viral (aseptic) meningitis. Transmission is fecal-oral, with peak incidence in summer and fall. CSF analysis shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and negative bacterial cultures.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with acute-onset high fever, temporal lobe seizures, olfactory hallucinations, and bizarre behavioral changes. Brain MRI demonstrates asymmetric hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR localized to the inferior and medial temporal lobes. What is the causative pathogen, and what is the urgent antiviral therapy?

options.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1); Intravenous acyclovir
JC virus; Highly active antiretroviral therapy

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1); Intravenous acyclovir.

Herpes Simplex Encephalitis (HSE):
• Etiology: HSV-1 (>90% of cases in adults, entering the brain via retrograde olfactory or trigeminal nerve transport).
• Hallmark features: Hemorrhagic necrotizing encephalitis localized to the temporal and inferior frontal lobes, presenting with fever, focal temporal seizures, aphasia, and olfactory hallucinations.
• Diagnostics: CSF HSV PCR is the test of choice.
• Treatment: Immediate empiric IV Acyclovir (inhibits viral DNA polymerase following phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase); delaying acyclovir dramatically increases mortality.

stem: Which virulence factor possessed by Streptococcus pneumoniae is a capsule composed of polysaccharides that inhibits phagocytosis by preventing complement factor C3b opsonization, serving as the basis for the PPSV23 and PCV20 vaccines?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Polysaccharide capsule.

Streptococcus pneumoniae possesses several virulence factors:
• Polysaccharide capsule: The most important virulence factor (>100 serotypes); physically shields the cell wall from opsonization by C3b, preventing neutrophil phagocytosis. Asplenic patients (sickle cell disease, splenectomy) lack splenic macrophage clearance of encapsulated bacteria and are at high risk of fatal pneumococcal sepsis/meningitis.
• IgA protease: Cleaves secretory IgA, facilitating mucosal colonization.
• Pneumolysin: Cytotoxin that forms pores in host membranes.

stem: Prior to performing a lumbar puncture on an adult with suspected bacterial meningitis, which of the following clinical criteria warrants an immediate non-contrast head CT to rule out intracranial mass effect and prevent brain herniation?

options.text: Focal neurological deficit, altered consciousness, new-onset seizure, papilledema, or immunocompromised state
Elevated peripheral white blood cell count

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Focal neurological deficit, altered consciousness, new-onset seizure, papilledema, or immunocompromised state.

Indications for head CT before LP in suspected meningitis ('FAILS'):
• F: Focal neurological deficit (e.g., hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsy)
• A: Altered mental status / consciousness (GCS < 15)
• I: Immunocompromised state (HIV, immunosuppressants, transplant)
• L: Lesion suspected / Papilledema (signs of elevated ICP)
• S: Seizure within past week.
In patients meeting these criteria, blood cultures and empiric antibiotics + dexamethasone must be administered IMMEDIATELY before taking the patient to the CT scanner.

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with tuberculous meningitis. Tuberculous meningitis characteristically causes a dense, gelatinous, inflammatory exudate that preferentially encases which anatomical region of the brain, leading to multiple cranial nerve palsies (CN III, IV, VI, VII) and communicating hydrocephalus?

options.text: Basal cisterns and base of the brain

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Basal cisterns and base of the brain.

Tuberculous (TB) meningitis (caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis) typically begins with the rupture of a subependymal Rich focus into the subarachnoid space. It characteristically forms a thick, gelatinous, granulomatous exudate that preferentially accumulates in the Basal Cisterns (interpeduncular, chiasmatic, and prepontine cisterns). This results in:
1. Entrapment and paralysis of cranial nerves coursing through the skull base (CN III, VI, VII).
2. Endarteritis obliterans of Circle of Willis vessels (causing stroke).
3. Obstructed arachnoid villi causing communicating hydrocephalus.

stem: Which of the following encapsulated Gram-negative coccobacilli was historically a leading cause of bacterial meningitis, epiglottitis, and septic arthritis in children between 6 months and 2 years of age, but has seen its incidence drop by >99% following the introduction of a conjugate vaccine containing its polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsular antigen?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).

Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib):
• Microbiology: Small, pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus requiring Factor X (hemin) and Factor V (NAD) to grow on chocolate agar.
• Capsule: Composed of Polyribosylribitol Phosphate (PRP).
• History: Prior to the Hib conjugate vaccine (PRP conjugated to diphtheria toxoid or tetanus toxoid to elicit T-cell dependent B-cell memory), it was the leading cause of pediatric meningitis. Sensorineural deafness was the most common long-term sequela.

stem: A 16-year-old girl in the intensive care unit with fulminant meningococcal meningitis develops refractory hypotension, widespread purpura fulminans, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and acute primary adrenal insufficiency. Autopsy reveals massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage and cortical necrosis. What is the eponymous name of this syndrome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is a catastrophic complication of severe meningococcemia (and rarely S. pneumoniae or Pseudomonas):
• Pathophysiology: Massive endotoxemia (lipooligosaccharide / LOS) causes widespread endothelial damage, severe DIC, and microvascular thrombosis.
• Pathology: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage with acute hemorrhagic infarction and destruction of the adrenal cortices.
• Clinical features: Profound refractory septic shock, severe hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and death within hours.

stem: Which of the following free-living amoebae is acquired by sniffing warm, contaminated freshwater lakes through the nose, penetrates the cribriform plate along olfactory nerves, and causes rapidly fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) within 3–7 days in healthy children and young adults?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Naegleria fowleri.

Naegleria fowleri (the 'brain-eating amoeba'):
• Transmission: Thermophilic free-living amoeba found in warm freshwater (lakes, rivers, unchlorinated pools, neti pots). Trophozoites enter the nasal cavity during swimming or diving.
• Invasion: Penetrates the nasal neuroepithelium, migrates through the cribriform plate along olfactory nerve fibers into the olfactory bulb and frontal lobes.
• Clinical course: Fulminant, purulent, hemorrhagic necrotizing meningoencephalitis (Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis / PAM); mortality >97%.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with fever, stiff neck, and bilateral tender swelling of the parotid glands (parotitis). Lumbar puncture shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose, consistent with aseptic meningitis. Which single-stranded, negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus with surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase is responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Mumps virus.

Mumps virus (Paramyxovirus family: enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA):
• Manifestations: Parotitis (bilateral painful salivary gland swelling), orchitis (testicular inflammation that can cause subfertility in postpubertal males), and aseptic meningitis (~10-30% of patients).
• Prevention: Live-attenuated MMR vaccine (Measles, Mumps, Rubella).

stem: In the empiric treatment of acute bacterial meningitis in an immunocompetent adult aged 18 to 50, standard guidelines recommend the combination of Vancomycin and Ceftriaxone. Why is Vancomycin included in this empiric regimen?

options.text: To provide broad coverage against Gram-negative bacilli
To cover penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae
To treat fungal organisms in the subarachnoid space

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. To cover penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Empiric antimicrobial rationale in adult bacterial meningitis:
• Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime): Excellent CSF penetration; covers Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae, and susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae.
• Vancomycin: Added routinely to empiric therapy to guarantee coverage against Cephalosporin-resistant strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae (mediated by altered penicillin-binding proteins, PBPs). (Vancomycin is stopped only if susceptibility testing confirms cephalosporin sensitivity).

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of mild, self-limiting lymphocytic meningitis (Mollaret meningitis) over the past 3 years. Between episodes, she is completely asymptomatic. PCR testing of her CSF during acute episodes is most likely to be positive for which viral pathogen?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2).

Mollaret meningitis is a syndrome of benign, recurrent, self-limiting aseptic meningitis:
• Etiology: Vast majority of cases are caused by reactivation of Herpes Simplex Virus type 2 (HSV-2) from sacral sensory ganglia.
• Distinct clinical contrast: While HSV-1 causes severe, focal temporal necrotizing encephalitis in adults, HSV-2 characteristically causes diffuse, non-focal aseptic meningitis and recurrent Mollaret meningitis.

stem: An adult patient with confirmed bacterial meningitis undergoes physical examination. Which of the following cranial nerves is most frequently affected in acute bacterial meningitis, leading to permanent sensorineural hearing loss as the most common long-term neurological sequela?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Cranial nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear).

Sensorineural hearing loss occurs in up to 10-30% of survivors of acute bacterial meningitis (especially pneumococcal meningitis):
• Pathophysiology: Suppurative inflammation spreads from the subarachnoid space through the cochlear aqueduct into the inner ear (suppurative labyrinthitis), damaging the delicate sensory hair cells of the organ of Corti and causing direct inflammatory neuritis of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).
• Early administration of dexamethasone significantly reduces this complication.
